# 08 — Inference Runtime **Scope:** how a serving system runs the model: the two phases of a request, the KV cache, batches, and the main speed techniques. **Previous:** [07 Output and sampling](07-output-and-sampling.md). **Next:** [09 Scaling across devices](09-scaling-across-devices.md). ## Components of a serving system Engines such as vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and llama.cpp share a similar structure: ```mermaid flowchart LR C[Client] --> API["API server
chat template, tokenizer"] API --> SCH["Scheduler
chooses which requests
run in the next step"] SCH --> EX["Model executor
forward pass on GPU"] EX <--> KV["KV cache manager
allocates cache blocks"] EX --> SMP["Sampler
(07)"] SMP --> DT["Detokenizer
streams text"] DT --> C SMP -.->|"new token"| SCH ``` The scheduler and the KV cache manager are the parts that most affect speed and cost. ## Two phases: prefill and decode Every request has two phases with very different hardware profiles ([NVIDIA, *Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization*](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/)). ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant R as Runtime participant G as GPU R->>G: Prefill: all prompt tokens in one pass G-->>R: KV cache filled + first output token loop Decode: once per output token R->>G: One new token + KV cache G-->>R: Next token, cache grows by one entry end ``` | | Prefill | Decode | |---|---------|--------| | Input per step | The whole prompt | One token per request | | Parallel work | High: all prompt tokens at once | Low: tokens depend on each other | | Bottleneck | **Compute** (arithmetic) | **Memory bandwidth** (data movement) | | User-visible metric | Time to first token (TTFT) | Time per output token (TPOT), also called inter-token latency | ## Why decode is memory-bound To produce one token, the GPU must read **every weight** from memory, plus the request's KV cache. But it does only about two arithmetic operations per weight ([02](02-tensors-and-weights.md)). The GPU's arithmetic units are fast, so they wait for memory. A rough estimate for one request alone: - Llama 2 7B in bf16 has about 13.5 GB of weights. - A data-center GPU reads memory at roughly 2 TB/s. - So one decode step takes at least 13.5 GB ÷ 2 TB/s ≈ 7 ms. That gives at most about 150 tokens per second. This estimate ignores the KV cache and other overhead, so real numbers are lower. It shows the key point: **for one request, speed depends on bytes moved, not on arithmetic.** ## Batches convert memory time into throughput If the server runs 32 requests in the same step, it reads the weights once and uses them 32 times. The step takes about the same time, but it produces 32 tokens. So batches raise throughput (total tokens per second) much more than they raise latency. This is the main economic lever of LLM serving. The limit is memory. Each request in the batch needs its own KV cache. ## The KV cache In each attention layer, the keys and values of earlier tokens do not change ([05](05-attention.md)). So the runtime stores them and reuses them at every decode step. This store is the **KV cache**. Some implementations keep one cache per layer ([NVIDIA](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/)). Properties: - **It is per-request state.** It is the only state the model keeps during a request ([00](00-big-picture.md)). - **It grows by one entry per token.** Llama 2 7B needs 512 KiB per token, so a 4,096-token context needs 2 GiB ([05](05-attention.md)). - **It competes with the weights for GPU memory.** The free memory after the weights load sets the maximum batch size and context length. ## Continuous batching Early systems ran a fixed batch until **all** its requests finished. A short request waited for the longest one, and new requests waited for the whole batch. [Orca (Yu et al., OSDI 2022)](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu) schedules at the level of **one iteration** instead. After each decode step, finished requests leave and new requests join. vLLM calls this "continuous batching". TensorRT-LLM calls it "in-flight batching". ## PagedAttention: virtual memory for the KV cache Before PagedAttention, systems reserved one contiguous memory region per request, sized for the maximum length. Most of this memory went unused, through fragmentation and over-reservation. [PagedAttention (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180) applies the operating-system idea of paging: - The cache is split into fixed-size **blocks**, like memory pages. - A per-request **block table** maps logical token positions to physical blocks, like a page table. - Blocks need not be contiguous, so external fragmentation disappears. - Requests can **share** blocks, for example when several outputs come from the same prompt. vLLM, built on PagedAttention, reported 2–4× higher throughput than earlier systems at the same latency. ## Other runtime techniques | Technique | Problem it solves | How | |-----------|-------------------|-----| | **Prefix caching** | Many requests share the same system prompt | Keep the KV cache of a common prefix and reuse it. This skips part of the prefill. | | **Chunked prefill** | A long prompt blocks decode steps of other requests | Split the prefill into chunks and mix them with decode steps ([NVIDIA](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/streamlining-ai-inference-performance-and-deployment-with-nvidia-tensorrt-llm-chunked-prefill/)). | | **Disaggregated serving** | Prefill and decode need different hardware profiles | Run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools and transfer the KV cache. | | **Speculative decoding** | Decode does one token per memory-bound step | A small draft model proposes several tokens. The large model checks them all in one pass. The output distribution stays the same as the large model's ([Leviathan et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)). | | **FlashAttention** | Attention memory traffic | Tile the computation in on-chip SRAM ([05](05-attention.md)). | | **Quantization** | Weight and cache size | Store numbers in fewer bits ([11](11-model-files-and-quantization.md)). | ## Sources - NVIDIA Technical Blog, *Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization* — https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/ - NVIDIA Technical Blog, *Streamlining AI Inference Performance and Deployment with NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM Chunked Prefill* — https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/streamlining-ai-inference-performance-and-deployment-with-nvidia-tensorrt-llm-chunked-prefill/ - Yu et al., *Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models*, OSDI 2022 — https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu - Kwon et al., *Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention*, SOSP 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180 - Leviathan, Kalman, Matias, *Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding*, ICML 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192 - Dao et al., *FlashAttention*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135 ======= # 09 — Scaling Across Devices **Scope:** how a model that does not fit on one GPU runs on many GPUs, for training and for inference. **Previous:** [08 Inference runtime](08-inference-runtime.md). **Next:** [10 Mixture of experts](10-mixture-of-experts.md). ## The problem Llama 2 70B needs about 140 GB for its weights in bf16 ([02](02-tensors-and-weights.md)). A large data-center GPU has 80 GB of memory. So the model does not fit on one GPU, even before the KV cache. Training needs much more memory: gradients and optimizer state add about 16 bytes per parameter in total with Adam and mixed precision ([Rajbhandari et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)). The fixed block structure ([04](04-transformer-block.md)) gives several natural places to split the work. ## The four main splits ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph DP["Data parallel: copy the model, split the requests or batch"] direction LR R1[Replica 1] ~~~ R2[Replica 2] end subgraph PP["Pipeline parallel: split the layers"] direction LR S1["GPU A
blocks 1–40"] --> S2["GPU B
blocks 41–80"] end subgraph TP["Tensor parallel: split each matrix"] direction LR T1["GPU A
heads 1–32"] <-->|all-reduce| T2["GPU B
heads 33–64"] end subgraph EP["Expert parallel (MoE only): split the experts"] direction LR E1["GPU A
experts 1–4"] <-->|all-to-all| E2["GPU B
experts 5–8"] end DP ~~~ PP ~~~ TP ~~~ EP ``` | Split | What each GPU holds | Communication | Best link | |-------|---------------------|---------------|-----------| | **Data parallel** | A full copy of the model | Training: average the gradients once per step. Inference: none. | Any | | **Tensor parallel** | A slice of every weight matrix | Two all-reduce operations per block, in every forward pass | Very fast (NVLink, inside one server) | | **Pipeline parallel** | A range of whole blocks | Send the activations to the next stage | Moderate (can cross servers) | | **Expert parallel** | A subset of the MoE experts | Send each token to its experts and back (all-to-all) | Fast | ## Tensor parallelism in detail [Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053) splits each block across GPUs with few synchronization points: - **Attention:** each GPU computes a subset of the heads. Heads are independent ([05](05-attention.md)), so this split needs no communication until the output projection. - **MLP:** the first matrix splits by columns, so each GPU applies the activation function to its own slice. The second matrix splits by rows. One all-reduce sums the partial results. The result is two all-reduce operations per block in the forward pass. Because this traffic happens in every block, tensor parallelism needs a very fast link. The later Megatron paper reports that tensor parallelism works well inside one 8-GPU server, but degrades across servers, where the links are slower ([Narayanan et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)). ## Pipeline parallelism in detail Pipeline parallelism puts consecutive blocks on consecutive GPUs, like stages of an assembly line. With one large batch, only one stage works at a time and the others wait. These idle periods are "bubbles". So the runtime splits the batch into micro-batches that flow through the stages one after another ([GPipe, Huang et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.06965)). ## Sharded data parallelism Plain data parallelism stores a full copy of the weights, gradients, and optimizer state on every GPU. This wastes memory. **ZeRO** ([Rajbhandari et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)) and PyTorch **FSDP** split these three kinds of state across the data-parallel GPUs. Each GPU collects the weights of a layer only when it needs them. ## The usual combination Large training runs combine the splits. This is often called "3D parallelism" ([Narayanan et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)): - Tensor parallel **inside** a server, over the fastest links. - Pipeline parallel **across** servers. - Data parallel across copies of this whole arrangement. For inference, a common layout is tensor parallel across the GPUs of one server. Data parallel replicas then handle more traffic. ## Sources - Shoeybi et al., *Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism*, 2019 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053 - Narayanan et al., *Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM*, SC 2021 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473 - Huang et al., *GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism*, NeurIPS 2019 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.06965 - Rajbhandari et al., *ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models*, SC 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 - PyTorch, *Getting Started with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)* — https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/FSDP_tutorial.html ======= # 10 — Mixture of Experts (MoE) **Scope:** models that keep many expert MLPs but run only a few of them for each token. **Previous:** [09 Scaling across devices](09-scaling-across-devices.md). **Next:** [11 Model files and quantization](11-model-files-and-quantization.md). ## The idea In a dense model, every token passes through every weight. In an MoE model, each block replaces its single MLP ([06](06-mlp-and-neurons.md)) with: - a set of **experts**: several independent MLPs, each a normal feed-forward block, and - a **router**: a small learned layer that picks which experts process each token. Attention, norms, and embeddings stay the same as in a dense model. The idea dates back to [Shazeer et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538). [GShard (Lepikhin et al., 2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668) and [Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) scaled it to transformers. ```mermaid flowchart TD IN["Token vector
(after attention)"] --> RT["Router
score for each expert"] RT -->|"top-2 chosen"| E2["Expert 2"] RT -->|"top-2 chosen"| E7["Expert 7"] RT -.->|"not chosen"| EO["Experts 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8
(idle for this token)"] E2 --> MIX(("weighted
sum")) E7 --> MIX MIX --> OUT["Add to residual stream"] ``` ## How the router works 1. The router computes a score for each expert from the token vector. 2. It keeps the **top-k** experts. Mixtral uses k = 2 ([Jiang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088)). Switch Transformer uses k = 1. 3. It converts the kept scores into weights. 4. The selected experts run. Their outputs combine as a weighted sum. The router decides **per token and per layer**. One token can use different experts in different layers. Neighbor tokens can use different experts in the same layer. ## Total versus active parameters MoE separates two numbers that are equal in a dense model: | Model | Total parameters | Active parameters per token | |-------|------------------|-----------------------------| | Mixtral 8x7B | about 47 B | about 13 B | The attention layers and embeddings are shared, so the total is less than 8 × 7 B. The system consequence: - **Compute per token follows the active count.** Mixtral costs about as much arithmetic per token as a 13 B dense model. - **Memory follows the total count.** All experts must stay loaded, because the next token can need any of them. Mixtral needs the memory of a 47 B model. So MoE trades memory for compute. It suits large servers more than small devices. ## System challenges | Challenge | Why it happens | Common response | |-----------|----------------|-----------------| | **Load imbalance** | The router can send most tokens to a few favorite experts. | An auxiliary **load-balancing loss** in training pushes the router toward an even spread ([Switch Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961)). | | **Capacity overflow** | Each expert has a fixed buffer per batch. | A **capacity factor** sets the buffer size. Switch Transformer drops tokens beyond the buffer from that layer's expert step. | | **Communication** | With expert parallelism, experts live on different GPUs ([09](09-scaling-across-devices.md)). | An **all-to-all** exchange sends each token to its experts and back, in every MoE layer. | | **Memory bandwidth in large batches** | Different tokens in a batch select different experts. So a large decode batch reads most experts in every step. | Expert parallelism and batch scheduling. | ## What experts specialize in The name "expert" suggests topic experts, such as a "math expert". The evidence does not support this simple picture. The Mixtral authors analyzed the router choices and report no clear pattern by topic. They saw more structure tied to syntax and to token position ([Jiang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088)). Treat an expert as a capacity unit that the router learned to use, not as a human-readable module. ## Sources - Shazeer et al., *Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer*, ICLR 2017 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538 - Lepikhin et al., *GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding*, 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668 - Fedus, Zoph, Shazeer, *Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity*, JMLR 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961 - Jiang et al., *Mixtral of Experts*, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088

The output distribution stays the same as the large model's ([Leviathan et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)). | | **FlashAttention** | Attention memory traffic | Tile the computation in on-chip SRAM ([05](05-attention.md)). | | **Quantization** | Weight and cache size | Store numbers in fewer bits ([11](11-model-files-and-quantization.md)). | ## Sources - NVIDIA Technical Blog, *Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization* — https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/mastering-llm-techniques-inference-optimization/ - NVIDIA Technical Blog, *Streamlining AI Inference Performance and Deployment with NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM Chunked Prefill* — https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/streamlining-ai-inference-performance-and-deployment-with-nvidia-tensorrt-llm-chunked-prefill/ - Yu et al., *Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models*, OSDI 2022 — https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu - Kwon et al., *Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention*, SOSP 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180 - Leviathan, Kalman, Matias, *Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding*, ICML 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192 - Dao et al., *FlashAttention*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135 ======= # 09 — Scaling Across Devices **Scope:** how a model that does not fit on one GPU runs on many GPUs, for training and for inference. **Previous:** [08 Inference runtime](08-inference-runtime.md). **Next:** [10 Mixture of experts](10-mixture-of-experts.md). ## The problem Llama 2 70B needs about 140 GB for its weights in bf16 ([02](02-tensors-and-weights.md)). A large data-center GPU has 80 GB of memory. So the model does not fit on one GPU, even before the KV cache. Training needs much more memory: gradients and optimizer state add about 16 bytes per parameter in total with Adam and mixed precision ([Rajbhandari et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)). The fixed block structure ([04](04-transformer-block.md)) gives several natural places to split the work. ## The four main splits ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph DP["Data parallel: copy the model, split the requests or batch"] direction LR R1[Replica 1] ~~~ R2[Replica 2] end subgraph PP["Pipeline parallel: split the layers"] direction LR S1["GPU A
blocks 1–40"] --> S2["GPU B
blocks 41–80"] end subgraph TP["Tensor parallel: split each matrix"] direction LR T1["GPU A
heads 1–32"] <-->|all-reduce| T2["GPU B
heads 33–64"] end subgraph EP["Expert parallel (MoE only): split the experts"] direction LR E1["GPU A
experts 1–4"] <-->|all-to-all| E2["GPU B
experts 5–8"] end DP ~~~ PP ~~~ TP ~~~ EP ``` | Split | What each GPU holds | Communication | Best link | |-------|---------------------|---------------|-----------| | **Data parallel** | A full copy of the model | Training: average the gradients once per step. Inference: none. | Any | | **Tensor parallel** | A slice of every weight matrix | Two all-reduce operations per block, in every forward pass | Very fast (NVLink, inside one server) | | **Pipeline parallel** | A range of whole blocks | Send the activations to the next stage | Moderate (can cross servers) | | **Expert parallel** | A subset of the MoE experts | Send each token to its experts and back (all-to-all) | Fast | ## Tensor parallelism in detail [Megatron-LM (Shoeybi et al., 2019)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053) splits each block across GPUs with few synchronization points: - **Attention:** each GPU computes a subset of the heads. Heads are independent ([05](05-attention.md)), so this split needs no communication until the output projection. - **MLP:** the first matrix splits by columns, so each GPU applies the activation function to its own slice. The second matrix splits by rows. One all-reduce sums the partial results. The result is two all-reduce operations per block in the forward pass. Because this traffic happens in every block, tensor parallelism needs a very fast link. The later Megatron paper reports that tensor parallelism works well inside one 8-GPU server, but degrades across servers, where the links are slower ([Narayanan et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)). ## Pipeline parallelism in detail Pipeline parallelism puts consecutive blocks on consecutive GPUs, like stages of an assembly line. With one large batch, only one stage works at a time and the others wait. These idle periods are "bubbles". So the runtime splits the batch into micro-batches that flow through the stages one after another ([GPipe, Huang et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.06965)). ## Sharded data parallelism Plain data parallelism stores a full copy of the weights, gradients, and optimizer state on every GPU. This wastes memory. **ZeRO** ([Rajbhandari et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)) and PyTorch **FSDP** split these three kinds of state across the data-parallel GPUs. Each GPU collects the weights of a layer only when it needs them. ## The usual combination Large training runs combine the splits. This is often called "3D parallelism" ([Narayanan et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473)): - Tensor parallel **inside** a server, over the fastest links. - Pipeline parallel **across** servers. - Data parallel across copies of this whole arrangement. For inference, a common layout is tensor parallel across the GPUs of one server. Data parallel replicas then handle more traffic. ## Sources - Shoeybi et al., *Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism*, 2019 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08053 - Narayanan et al., *Efficient Large-Scale Language Model Training on GPU Clusters Using Megatron-LM*, SC 2021 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04473 - Huang et al., *GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism*, NeurIPS 2019 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.06965 - Rajbhandari et al., *ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models*, SC 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 - PyTorch, *Getting Started with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)* — https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/FSDP_tutorial.html ======= # 10 — Mixture of Experts (MoE) **Scope:** models that keep many expert MLPs but run only a few of them for each token. **Previous:** [09 Scaling across devices](09-scaling-across-devices.md). **Next:** [11 Model files and quantization](11-model-files-and-quantization.md). ## The idea In a dense model, every token passes through every weight. In an MoE model, each block replaces its single MLP ([06](06-mlp-and-neurons.md)) with: - a set of **experts**: several independent MLPs, each a normal feed-forward block, and - a **router**: a small learned layer that picks which experts process each token. Attention, norms, and embeddings stay the same as in a dense model. The idea dates back to [Shazeer et al. (2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538). [GShard (Lepikhin et al., 2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668) and [Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) scaled it to transformers. ```mermaid flowchart TD IN["Token vector
(after attention)"] --> RT["Router
score for each expert"] RT -->|"top-2 chosen"| E2["Expert 2"] RT -->|"top-2 chosen"| E7["Expert 7"] RT -.->|"not chosen"| EO["Experts 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8
(idle for this token)"] E2 --> MIX(("weighted
sum")) E7 --> MIX MIX --> OUT["Add to residual stream"] ``` ## How the router works 1. The router computes a score for each expert from the token vector. 2. It keeps the **top-k** experts. Mixtral uses k = 2 ([Jiang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088)). Switch Transformer uses k = 1. 3. It converts the kept scores into weights. 4. The selected experts run. Their outputs combine as a weighted sum. The router decides **per token and per layer**. One token can use different experts in different layers. Neighbor tokens can use different experts in the same layer. ## Total versus active parameters MoE separates two numbers that are equal in a dense model: | Model | Total parameters | Active parameters per token | |-------|------------------|-----------------------------| | Mixtral 8x7B | about 47 B | about 13 B | The attention layers and embeddings are shared, so the total is less than 8 × 7 B. The system consequence: - **Compute per token follows the active count.** Mixtral costs about as much arithmetic per token as a 13 B dense model. - **Memory follows the total count.** All experts must stay loaded, because the next token can need any of them. Mixtral needs the memory of a 47 B model. So MoE trades memory for compute. It suits large servers more than small devices. ## System challenges | Challenge | Why it happens | Common response | |-----------|----------------|-----------------| | **Load imbalance** | The router can send most tokens to a few favorite experts. | An auxiliary **load-balancing loss** in training pushes the router toward an even spread ([Switch Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961)). | | **Capacity overflow** | Each expert has a fixed buffer per batch. | A **capacity factor** sets the buffer size. Switch Transformer drops tokens beyond the buffer from that layer's expert step. | | **Communication** | With expert parallelism, experts live on different GPUs ([09](09-scaling-across-devices.md)). | An **all-to-all** exchange sends each token to its experts and back, in every MoE layer. | | **Memory bandwidth in large batches** | Different tokens in a batch select different experts. So a large decode batch reads most experts in every step. | Expert parallelism and batch scheduling. | ## What experts specialize in The name "expert" suggests topic experts, such as a "math expert". The evidence does not support this simple picture. The Mixtral authors analyzed the router choices and report no clear pattern by topic. They saw more structure tied to syntax and to token position ([Jiang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088)). Treat an expert as a capacity unit that the router learned to use, not as a human-readable module. ## Sources - Shazeer et al., *Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer*, ICLR 2017 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538 - Lepikhin et al., *GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding*, 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16668 - Fedus, Zoph, Shazeer, *Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity*, JMLR 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961 - Jiang et al., *Mixtral of Experts*, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088

# 02 — Tensors and Weights **Scope:** the data structure that holds the model, the four kinds of memory an LLM uses, and how to compute a model's size. **Previous:** [01 Tokenizer](01-tokenizer.md). **Next:** [03 Embeddings and positions](03-embeddings-and-positions.md). ## What a tensor is A tensor is a multi-dimensional array of numbers of one type. Every piece of data inside an LLM is a tensor: the weights, the token vectors, and the cache. PyTorch describes a tensor as a **storage** plus **metadata** ([PyTorch docs, storage](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/storage.html); [tensor attributes](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensor_attributes.html)): | Part | Meaning | Example | |------|---------|---------| | Storage | One flat, contiguous block of bytes | 33,554,432 bytes | | dtype | The number format of each element | `bfloat16` | | Shape | The size of each dimension | `(4096, 4096)` | | Stride | How many elements to skip to move one step in each dimension | `(4096, 1)` | | Offset | Where the tensor starts inside the storage | `0` | | Device | Where the storage lives | `cuda:0` | This split is a systems design choice. A transpose or a slice changes only the metadata. It creates a new **view** of the same storage, with no data copy. ## The four kinds of memory An LLM process holds four different kinds of tensor. Each kind has a different lifetime and a different owner. | Kind | What it holds | Lifetime | Size depends on | Document | |------|---------------|----------|-----------------|----------| | **Weights** (parameters) | The learned numbers | Fixed after training; loaded once | Model architecture | this page | | **Activations** | The intermediate vectors of one forward pass | One pass | Batch size × sequence length × model dimension | [04](04-transformer-block.md) | | **KV cache** | Saved attention keys and values for earlier tokens | One request or conversation | Tokens in context × layers × KV heads | [08](08-inference-runtime.md) | | **Optimizer state** | Gradients, master weights, and optimizer moments | Training only | Parameter count (about 16 bytes per parameter in total with Adam and mixed precision) | [12](12-training-lifecycle.md) | For inference, the weights and the KV cache take nearly all GPU memory. ## Shapes inside the model The main activation tensor has the shape `[batch, sequence length, model dimension]`. Each row along the last dimension is the vector for one token. Every block reads a tensor of this shape and writes a tensor of the same shape (see [04](04-transformer-block.md)). Most weights are 2-D matrices. A matrix with shape `[input size, output size]` converts a vector of one length into a vector of another length. Matrix multiplication is the dominant operation in an LLM, and GPUs are built to do it fast. ## Number formats (dtypes) | dtype | Bytes per number | Notes | |-------|------------------|-------| | float32 (fp32) | 4 | The full-precision reference format. | | float16 (fp16) | 2 | 5 exponent bits. Small range: the maximum is about 65,504. | | bfloat16 (bf16) | 2 | 8 exponent bits, the same range as fp32, with less precision. Google designed it for TPUs ([Google Cloud blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/bfloat16-the-secret-to-high-performance-on-cloud-tpus)). Most modern LLMs train in bf16. | | int8 | 1 | Used for quantized weights. See [11](11-model-files-and-quantization.md). | | 4-bit | 0.5 | Used for quantized weights. Needs a scale factor per block of numbers. | ## Where the parameters are: a worked count Llama 2 7B has 32 layers, a model dimension of 4,096, an MLP width of 11,008, and a vocabulary of 32,000. The count below uses only these values. | Part | Calculation | Parameters | |------|-------------|------------| | Embedding table ([03](03-embeddings-and-positions.md)) | 32,000 × 4,096 | 131 M | | Attention, per layer ([05](05-attention.md)) | 4 matrices × 4,096 × 4,096 | 67 M | | MLP, per layer ([06](06-mlp-and-neurons.md)) | 3 matrices × 4,096 × 11,008 | 135 M | | Norms, per layer | 2 × 4,096 | 0.008 M | | **All 32 layers** | 32 × 202 M | 6,480 M | | Output head ([07](07-output-and-sampling.md)) | 4,096 × 32,000 | 131 M | | **Total** | | **about 6.74 B** | Three observations: 1. **The MLP layers hold about two thirds of the per-layer weights.** [Geva et al. (2021)](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446) report the same two-thirds share for transformers in general. 2. **The norms are tiny.** They have almost no parameters. 3. **The vocabulary matters.** The embedding table and output head together hold 262 M parameters here. With a 128K vocabulary, they hold four times as many. ## From parameter count to memory and compute - **Memory for weights** = parameters × bytes per parameter. Llama 2 7B in bf16 needs 6.74 B × 2 = about 13.5 GB. Llama 2 70B needs about 140 GB. - **Compute per token** is about 2 × parameters floating-point operations for a forward pass. This is a standard estimate ([Kaplan et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)). One multiply and one add for each weight. - **Memory traffic per token** matters more than compute in text generation. To produce one token, the GPU must read every weight once. [08 Inference runtime](08-inference-runtime.md) explains why this sets the speed limit. ## Sources - PyTorch documentation, *torch.Storage* — https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/storage.html - PyTorch documentation, *Tensor Attributes* — https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensor_attributes.html - Google Cloud, *BFloat16: The secret to high performance on Cloud TPUs* — https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/bfloat16-the-secret-to-high-performance-on-cloud-tpus - Higham, *What Is Bfloat16 Arithmetic?* — https://nhigham.com/2020/06/02/what-is-bfloat16-arithmetic/ - Touvron et al., *Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models*, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288 - Geva et al., *Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories*, EMNLP 2021 — https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446 - Kaplan et al., *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361 ======= # 03 — Embeddings and Positions **Scope:** how a token ID becomes a vector, and how the model knows the order of tokens. **Previous:** [02 Tensors and weights](02-tensors-and-weights.md). **Next:** [04 Transformer block](04-transformer-block.md). ## The embedding table The embedding table is a weight matrix with one row for each vocabulary entry. Its shape is `[vocabulary size, model dimension]`. For Llama 2 7B, the shape is `[32,000, 4,096]`. The operation is a table lookup: ``` token ID 8415 -> row 8415 of the table -> a vector of 4,096 numbers ``` The lookup is cheap. It reads one row per token and does no arithmetic. But the table is large, because it has one row for each vocabulary entry (see [01](01-tokenizer.md)). ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Token IDs
[791, 8415, 7731]"] --> B["Embedding table
[vocab × d_model]"] B --> C["Token vectors
[3 × d_model]"] C --> D["Residual stream
(04)"] ``` ## What the vector means Training sets the numbers in each row. Nobody designs them by hand. After training, directions in the vector space tend to correspond to properties. Tokens with related meaning get nearby vectors. 3Blue1Brown shows this with examples such as a "gender" direction ([*But what is a GPT?*, chapter 5](https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/neural-networks)). The embedding vector is only the starting point. Each block of the stack adds information to it, so the vector for "bank" soon carries different content in "river bank" and in "bank account". See [04](04-transformer-block.md). ## Shared input and output tables Some models use the same matrix for the embedding table and for the output head ([07](07-output-and-sampling.md)). This is "weight tying". GPT-2 ties the two matrices. Llama 2 does not. Tying saves one `[vocabulary × model dimension]` matrix. For a model with a large vocabulary, this saving is significant. ## Why the model needs position information The attention operation ([05](05-attention.md)) treats its input as a set. Without extra information, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" produce the same attention result. So every design adds position information. The designs differ in **where** they add it. | Method | Where it acts | Used by | Context limit | |--------|---------------|---------|---------------| | Sinusoidal absolute | A fixed vector added to each token vector at the input | Original transformer ([Vaswani et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)) | Soft | | Learned absolute | A learned vector per position, added at the input | GPT-2 | Hard: one row per position, so no input beyond the table size | | **RoPE** (rotary) | A rotation applied to queries and keys inside **every** attention layer | Llama 2, Llama 3, Mistral, many others | Soft; the runtime can stretch it | | ALiBi | A distance penalty added to attention scores | BLOOM | Soft | ## RoPE in system terms RoPE comes from [Su et al. (2021), RoFormer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864). It rotates each query vector and each key vector by an angle that depends on the token's position. Different pairs of dimensions rotate at different speeds. When attention compares a query with a key, the two rotations partly cancel. The result depends on the **distance** between the two tokens, not on their absolute positions. System consequences: - **RoPE has no weights.** It is a fixed function of the position. Nothing extra goes in the weights file, except a few settings in `config.json`, such as the base frequency. - **RoPE acts on the query and key vectors only.** It does not change the value vectors or the residual stream ([Llama 2 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288)). - **The cache stores rotated keys.** The KV cache ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)) holds keys after the rotation, so the runtime does not rotate them again. - **The context window can grow after training.** Methods such as position interpolation ([Chen et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15595)) rescale the positions so a model can accept longer inputs than in training. Quality outside the trained length is not guaranteed. ## Sources - Vaswani et al., *Attention Is All You Need*, 2017 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 - Su et al., *RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding*, 2021 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864 - Press, Smith, Lewis, *Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi)*, ICLR 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409 - Chen et al., *Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation*, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15595 - Touvron et al., *Llama 2*, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288 - 3Blue1Brown, *But what is a GPT? Visual intro to transformers* (Deep Learning, chapter 5) — https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/neural-networks ======= # 04 — Transformer Block and Residual Stream **Scope:** the repeated unit of an LLM, and the shared channel that its parts use to communicate. **Previous:** [03 Embeddings and positions](03-embeddings-and-positions.md). **Next:** [05 Attention](05-attention.md). ## The stack An LLM is a stack of identical **blocks** (also called layers). Llama 3 8B has 32 blocks. Llama 3 70B has 80 ([Llama 3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)). All blocks have the same structure but different weights. Each block reads a tensor of shape `[tokens, model dimension]` and writes a tensor of the same shape. This fixed interface has system benefits: - The runtime can run the blocks in a simple loop. - A pipeline-parallel runtime can put different blocks on different GPUs ([09](09-scaling-across-devices.md)). - The blocks run in strict sequence. So the latency of one forward pass grows with the number of blocks. ## Inside one block Modern decoder-only models use the "pre-norm" layout. Llama 2 uses pre-normalization with RMSNorm, a SwiGLU MLP, and RoPE ([Llama 2 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288)). ```mermaid flowchart TD IN["Residual stream in
[tokens × d_model]"] --> N1[RMSNorm] N1 --> ATT["Attention (05)
moves information between tokens"] ATT --> ADD1(("+")) IN --> ADD1 ADD1 --> N2[RMSNorm] N2 --> MLP["MLP (06)
processes each token alone"] MLP --> ADD2(("+")) ADD1 --> ADD2 ADD2 --> OUT["Residual stream out
[tokens × d_model]"] ``` The block has two sub-layers. Each sub-layer reads a normalized copy of the stream, computes an update, and **adds** the update back to the stream. | Sub-layer | Works across tokens? | Job | |-----------|----------------------|-----| | Attention | Yes | Copies information from earlier tokens into the current token. | | MLP | No, one token at a time | Transforms the information that is already in the token's vector. | This is the central division of labor in a transformer: **attention moves information, the MLP processes it.** ## The residual stream is a shared bus [Elhage et al. (2021)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html) describe the residual stream as a communication channel: - The stream does no processing itself. - Each attention layer and each MLP layer **reads** from the stream with a linear projection. - Each layer **writes** its result back by **adding** a linear projection to the stream. - So a later layer can read what any earlier layer wrote. Layers communicate only through the stream. A system analogy: the residual stream is a shared memory bus, or a blackboard. Every component reads the blackboard and adds notes to it. No component erases the blackboard. The stream width (the model dimension) is the bandwidth of the bus. Two consequences: 1. **Each layer is a small, additive change.** The final vector is the sum of the original embedding and every layer's contribution. Interpretability research uses this property to trace which component contributed what. See [13](13-interpretability.md). 2. **The bus is crowded.** Many layers write many kinds of information into the same fixed-width vector. Models pack more "features" than dimensions into it. This is "superposition". See [13](13-interpretability.md). ## Normalization A normalization layer rescales a vector to a standard size. It keeps the numbers in a stable range, so training does not diverge. - **LayerNorm** subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation. Then it applies a learned scale and shift. - **RMSNorm** ([Zhang and Sennrich, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467)) skips the mean step and the shift. It is cheaper, and Llama, Mistral, and many others use it. - **Pre-norm** puts the norm before each sub-layer, inside the branch. The stream itself stays un-normalized. Pre-norm makes deep stacks easier to train ([Xiong et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745)). A final norm runs after the last block and before the output head ([07](07-output-and-sampling.md)). ## What changes with depth Research finds a rough progression through the stack: - **Early layers** respond to surface patterns, such as specific words or n-grams ([Geva et al., 2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446)). - **Middle layers** hold more abstract features. Anthropic trained its large sparse autoencoders on a middle layer of Claude 3 Sonnet for this reason ([Templeton et al., 2024](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/index.html)). - **Late layers** focus on the prediction of the next token ([Geva et al., 2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446)). These are tendencies, not strict rules. ## Sources - Elhage et al., *A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits*, Anthropic, 2021 — https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html - Touvron et al., *Llama 2*, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288 - Llama Team, *The Llama 3 Herd of Models*, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783 - Zhang and Sennrich, *Root Mean Square Layer Normalization*, NeurIPS 2019 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467 - Xiong et al., *On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture*, ICML 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745 - Geva et al., *Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories*, EMNLP 2021 — https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446 - Templeton et al., *Scaling Monosemanticity*, Anthropic, 2024 — https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/index.html

PyTorch describes a tensor as a **storage** plus **metadata** ([PyTorch docs, storage](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/storage.html); [tensor attributes](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensor_attributes.html)): | Part | Meaning | Example | |------|---------|---------| | Storage | One flat, contiguous block of bytes | 33,554,432 bytes | | dtype | The number format of each element | `bfloat16` | | Shape | The size of each dimension | `(4096, 4096)` | | Stride | How many elements to skip to move one step in each dimension | `(4096, 1)` | | Offset | Where the tensor starts inside the storage | `0` | | Device | Where the storage lives | `cuda:0` | This split is a systems design choice. A transpose or a slice changes only the metadata. It creates a new **view** of the same storage, with no data copy. ## The four kinds of memory An LLM process holds four different kinds of tensor. Each kind has a different lifetime and a different owner. | Kind | What it holds | Lifetime | Size depends on | Document | |------|---------------|----------|-----------------|----------| | **Weights** (parameters) | The learned numbers | Fixed after training; loaded once | Model architecture | this page | | **Activations** | The intermediate vectors of one forward pass | One pass | Batch size × sequence length × model dimension | [04](04-transformer-block.md) | | **KV cache** | Saved attention keys and values for earlier tokens | One request or conversation | Tokens in context × layers × KV heads | [08](08-inference-runtime.md) | | **Optimizer state** | Gradients, master weights, and optimizer moments | Training only | Parameter count (about 16 bytes per parameter in total with Adam and mixed precision) | [12](12-training-lifecycle.md) | For inference, the weights and the KV cache take nearly all GPU memory. ## Shapes inside the model The main activation tensor has the shape `[batch, sequence length, model dimension]`. Each row along the last dimension is the vector for one token. Every block reads a tensor of this shape and writes a tensor of the same shape (see [04](04-transformer-block.md)). Most weights are 2-D matrices. A matrix with shape `[input size, output size]` converts a vector of one length into a vector of another length. Matrix multiplication is the dominant operation in an LLM, and GPUs are built to do it fast. ## Number formats (dtypes) | dtype | Bytes per number | Notes | |-------|------------------|-------| | float32 (fp32) | 4 | The full-precision reference format. | | float16 (fp16) | 2 | 5 exponent bits. Small range: the maximum is about 65,504. | | bfloat16 (bf16) | 2 | 8 exponent bits, the same range as fp32, with less precision. Google designed it for TPUs ([Google Cloud blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/bfloat16-the-secret-to-high-performance-on-cloud-tpus)). Most modern LLMs train in bf16. | | int8 | 1 | Used for quantized weights. See [11](11-model-files-and-quantization.md). | | 4-bit | 0.5 | Used for quantized weights. Needs a scale factor per block of numbers. | ## Where the parameters are: a worked count Llama 2 7B has 32 layers, a model dimension of 4,096, an MLP width of 11,008, and a vocabulary of 32,000. The count below uses only these values. | Part | Calculation | Parameters | |------|-------------|------------| | Embedding table ([03](03-embeddings-and-positions.md)) | 32,000 × 4,096 | 131 M | | Attention, per layer ([05](05-attention.md)) | 4 matrices × 4,096 × 4,096 | 67 M | | MLP, per layer ([06](06-mlp-and-neurons.md)) | 3 matrices × 4,096 × 11,008 | 135 M | | Norms, per layer | 2 × 4,096 | 0.008 M | | **All 32 layers** | 32 × 202 M | 6,480 M | | Output head ([07](07-output-and-sampling.md)) | 4,096 × 32,000 | 131 M | | **Total** | | **about 6.74 B** | Three observations: 1. **The MLP layers hold about two thirds of the per-layer weights.** [Geva et al. (2021)](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446) report the same two-thirds share for transformers in general. 2. **The norms are tiny.** They have almost no parameters. 3. **The vocabulary matters.** The embedding table and output head together hold 262 M parameters here. With a 128K vocabulary, they hold four times as many. ## From parameter count to memory and compute - **Memory for weights** = parameters × bytes per parameter. Llama 2 7B in bf16 needs 6.74 B × 2 = about 13.5 GB. Llama 2 70B needs about 140 GB. - **Compute per token** is about 2 × parameters floating-point operations for a forward pass. This is a standard estimate ([Kaplan et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)). One multiply and one add for each weight. - **Memory traffic per token** matters more than compute in text generation. To produce one token, the GPU must read every weight once. [08 Inference runtime](08-inference-runtime.md) explains why this sets the speed limit. ## Sources - PyTorch documentation, *torch.Storage* — https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/storage.html - PyTorch documentation, *Tensor Attributes* — https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensor_attributes.html - Google Cloud, *BFloat16: The secret to high performance on Cloud TPUs* — https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/bfloat16-the-secret-to-high-performance-on-cloud-tpus - Higham, *What Is Bfloat16 Arithmetic?* — https://nhigham.com/2020/06/02/what-is-bfloat16-arithmetic/ - Touvron et al., *Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models*, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288 - Geva et al., *Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories*, EMNLP 2021 — https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446 - Kaplan et al., *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361 ======= # 03 — Embeddings and Positions **Scope:** how a token ID becomes a vector, and how the model knows the order of tokens. **Previous:** [02 Tensors and weights](02-tensors-and-weights.md). **Next:** [04 Transformer block](04-transformer-block.md). ## The embedding table The embedding table is a weight matrix with one row for each vocabulary entry. Its shape is `[vocabulary size, model dimension]`. For Llama 2 7B, the shape is `[32,000, 4,096]`. The operation is a table lookup: ``` token ID 8415 -> row 8415 of the table -> a vector of 4,096 numbers ``` The lookup is cheap. It reads one row per token and does no arithmetic. But the table is large, because it has one row for each vocabulary entry (see [01](01-tokenizer.md)). ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Token IDs
[791, 8415, 7731]"] --> B["Embedding table
[vocab × d_model]"] B --> C["Token vectors
[3 × d_model]"] C --> D["Residual stream
(04)"] ``` ## What the vector means Training sets the numbers in each row. Nobody designs them by hand. After training, directions in the vector space tend to correspond to properties. Tokens with related meaning get nearby vectors. 3Blue1Brown shows this with examples such as a "gender" direction ([*But what is a GPT?*, chapter 5](https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/neural-networks)). The embedding vector is only the starting point. Each block of the stack adds information to it, so the vector for "bank" soon carries different content in "river bank" and in "bank account". See [04](04-transformer-block.md). ## Shared input and output tables Some models use the same matrix for the embedding table and for the output head ([07](07-output-and-sampling.md)). This is "weight tying". GPT-2 ties the two matrices. Llama 2 does not. Tying saves one `[vocabulary × model dimension]` matrix. For a model with a large vocabulary, this saving is significant. ## Why the model needs position information The attention operation ([05](05-attention.md)) treats its input as a set. Without extra information, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" produce the same attention result. So every design adds position information. The designs differ in **where** they add it. | Method | Where it acts | Used by | Context limit | |--------|---------------|---------|---------------| | Sinusoidal absolute | A fixed vector added to each token vector at the input | Original transformer ([Vaswani et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)) | Soft | | Learned absolute | A learned vector per position, added at the input | GPT-2 | Hard: one row per position, so no input beyond the table size | | **RoPE** (rotary) | A rotation applied to queries and keys inside **every** attention layer | Llama 2, Llama 3, Mistral, many others | Soft; the runtime can stretch it | | ALiBi | A distance penalty added to attention scores | BLOOM | Soft | ## RoPE in system terms RoPE comes from [Su et al. (2021), RoFormer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864). It rotates each query vector and each key vector by an angle that depends on the token's position. Different pairs of dimensions rotate at different speeds. When attention compares a query with a key, the two rotations partly cancel. The result depends on the **distance** between the two tokens, not on their absolute positions. System consequences: - **RoPE has no weights.** It is a fixed function of the position. Nothing extra goes in the weights file, except a few settings in `config.json`, such as the base frequency. - **RoPE acts on the query and key vectors only.** It does not change the value vectors or the residual stream ([Llama 2 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288)). - **The cache stores rotated keys.** The KV cache ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)) holds keys after the rotation, so the runtime does not rotate them again. - **The context window can grow after training.** Methods such as position interpolation ([Chen et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15595)) rescale the positions so a model can accept longer inputs than in training. Quality outside the trained length is not guaranteed. ## Sources - Vaswani et al., *Attention Is All You Need*, 2017 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 - Su et al., *RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding*, 2021 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864 - Press, Smith, Lewis, *Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi)*, ICLR 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12409 - Chen et al., *Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation*, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15595 - Touvron et al., *Llama 2*, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288 - 3Blue1Brown, *But what is a GPT? Visual intro to transformers* (Deep Learning, chapter 5) — https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/neural-networks ======= # 04 — Transformer Block and Residual Stream **Scope:** the repeated unit of an LLM, and the shared channel that its parts use to communicate. **Previous:** [03 Embeddings and positions](03-embeddings-and-positions.md). **Next:** [05 Attention](05-attention.md). ## The stack An LLM is a stack of identical **blocks** (also called layers). Llama 3 8B has 32 blocks. Llama 3 70B has 80 ([Llama 3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)). All blocks have the same structure but different weights. Each block reads a tensor of shape `[tokens, model dimension]` and writes a tensor of the same shape. This fixed interface has system benefits: - The runtime can run the blocks in a simple loop. - A pipeline-parallel runtime can put different blocks on different GPUs ([09](09-scaling-across-devices.md)). - The blocks run in strict sequence. So the latency of one forward pass grows with the number of blocks. ## Inside one block Modern decoder-only models use the "pre-norm" layout. Llama 2 uses pre-normalization with RMSNorm, a SwiGLU MLP, and RoPE ([Llama 2 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288)). ```mermaid flowchart TD IN["Residual stream in
[tokens × d_model]"] --> N1[RMSNorm] N1 --> ATT["Attention (05)
moves information between tokens"] ATT --> ADD1(("+")) IN --> ADD1 ADD1 --> N2[RMSNorm] N2 --> MLP["MLP (06)
processes each token alone"] MLP --> ADD2(("+")) ADD1 --> ADD2 ADD2 --> OUT["Residual stream out
[tokens × d_model]"] ``` The block has two sub-layers. Each sub-layer reads a normalized copy of the stream, computes an update, and **adds** the update back to the stream. | Sub-layer | Works across tokens? | Job | |-----------|----------------------|-----| | Attention | Yes | Copies information from earlier tokens into the current token. | | MLP | No, one token at a time | Transforms the information that is already in the token's vector. | This is the central division of labor in a transformer: **attention moves information, the MLP processes it.** ## The residual stream is a shared bus [Elhage et al. (2021)](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html) describe the residual stream as a communication channel: - The stream does no processing itself. - Each attention layer and each MLP layer **reads** from the stream with a linear projection. - Each layer **writes** its result back by **adding** a linear projection to the stream. - So a later layer can read what any earlier layer wrote. Layers communicate only through the stream. A system analogy: the residual stream is a shared memory bus, or a blackboard. Every component reads the blackboard and adds notes to it. No component erases the blackboard. The stream width (the model dimension) is the bandwidth of the bus. Two consequences: 1. **Each layer is a small, additive change.** The final vector is the sum of the original embedding and every layer's contribution. Interpretability research uses this property to trace which component contributed what. See [13](13-interpretability.md). 2. **The bus is crowded.** Many layers write many kinds of information into the same fixed-width vector. Models pack more "features" than dimensions into it. This is "superposition". See [13](13-interpretability.md). ## Normalization A normalization layer rescales a vector to a standard size. It keeps the numbers in a stable range, so training does not diverge. - **LayerNorm** subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation. Then it applies a learned scale and shift. - **RMSNorm** ([Zhang and Sennrich, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467)) skips the mean step and the shift. It is cheaper, and Llama, Mistral, and many others use it. - **Pre-norm** puts the norm before each sub-layer, inside the branch. The stream itself stays un-normalized. Pre-norm makes deep stacks easier to train ([Xiong et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745)). A final norm runs after the last block and before the output head ([07](07-output-and-sampling.md)). ## What changes with depth Research finds a rough progression through the stack: - **Early layers** respond to surface patterns, such as specific words or n-grams ([Geva et al., 2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446)). - **Middle layers** hold more abstract features. Anthropic trained its large sparse autoencoders on a middle layer of Claude 3 Sonnet for this reason ([Templeton et al., 2024](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/index.html)). - **Late layers** focus on the prediction of the next token ([Geva et al., 2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446)). These are tendencies, not strict rules. ## Sources - Elhage et al., *A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits*, Anthropic, 2021 — https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html - Touvron et al., *Llama 2*, 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288 - Llama Team, *The Llama 3 Herd of Models*, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783 - Zhang and Sennrich, *Root Mean Square Layer Normalization*, NeurIPS 2019 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.07467 - Xiong et al., *On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture*, ICML 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745 - Geva et al., *Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories*, EMNLP 2021 — https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446 - Templeton et al., *Scaling Monosemanticity*, Anthropic, 2024 — https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/index.html

# 11 — Model Files and Quantization **Scope:** what a model looks like on disk, the two main file formats, and how quantization shrinks a model. **Previous:** [10 Mixture of experts](10-mixture-of-experts.md). **Next:** [12 Training lifecycle](12-training-lifecycle.md). ## A model repository on disk A model in the Hugging Face layout is a folder of plain files. Each file maps to a component in this document set: | File | Contents | Component | |------|----------|-----------| | `config.json` | Architecture settings: layers, model dimension, heads, KV heads, MLP width, vocabulary size, RoPE settings | The graph shape ([00](00-big-picture.md)) | | `tokenizer.json` | Vocabulary, merge rules, normalizer, pre-tokenizer | [01 Tokenizer](01-tokenizer.md) | | `tokenizer_config.json` | Special tokens and the **chat template** | [01 Tokenizer](01-tokenizer.md) | | `generation_config.json` | Default sampler settings, such as temperature and stop tokens | [07 Sampling](07-output-and-sampling.md) | | `model-00001-of-00004.safetensors` … | The weight tensors, split into shards | [02 Tensors and weights](02-tensors-and-weights.md) | | `model.safetensors.index.json` | A map from each tensor name to its shard file | — | The config and the weights must agree. The runtime builds the empty graph from `config.json`, then fills it with tensors by name. ## Tensor names show the architecture Each tensor has a path-like name. A Llama-style model uses names like these: ``` model.embed_tokens.weight # embedding table (03) model.layers.0.input_layernorm.weight # RMSNorm before attention (04) model.layers.0.self_attn.q_proj.weight # W_Q (05) model.layers.0.self_attn.k_proj.weight # W_K (05) model.layers.0.self_attn.v_proj.weight # W_V (05) model.layers.0.self_attn.o_proj.weight # W_O (05) model.layers.0.post_attention_layernorm.weight model.layers.0.mlp.gate_proj.weight # SwiGLU gate (06) model.layers.0.mlp.up_proj.weight # SwiGLU up (06) model.layers.0.mlp.down_proj.weight # SwiGLU down (06) ... # layers 1 to N-1 model.norm.weight # final norm (07) lm_head.weight # output head (07) ``` A list of tensor names and shapes is a reliable way to learn a model's real architecture. ## safetensors [safetensors](https://github.com/huggingface/safetensors) is the standard weight format on the Hugging Face Hub. Its layout: 1. **8 bytes:** the length of the header. 2. **JSON header:** for each tensor, its name, dtype, shape, and byte offsets. An optional `__metadata__` entry holds string key-value pairs. 3. **Data:** the raw tensor bytes, back to back. Design properties: - **No code execution.** The older PyTorch format uses Python pickle, which can run arbitrary code at load time. In February 2024, JFrog reported models on the Hugging Face Hub whose pickle files opened a remote shell for the attacker when a user loaded them. safetensors contains only data. - **Memory mapping.** The runtime can map the file into memory and load each tensor only when it needs it. - **Cheap inspection.** A tool can read only the header, even over HTTP range requests, to list the tensors without a download of the weights ([safetensors docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/safetensors/metadata_parsing)). ## GGUF [GGUF](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md) is the format of llama.cpp and the ggml library. It puts **everything in one file**: architecture settings, tokenizer, chat template, and weights. Its layout is a magic number, a version, typed key-value metadata (for example `general.architecture`, `{arch}.block_count`, and `tokenizer.ggml.*` keys), tensor descriptors, and aligned tensor data that the runtime can memory-map. GGUF targets local inference. Its file names often carry the quantization type, such as `Q4_K_M` or `Q8_0`. ## Quantization Quantization stores numbers in fewer bits. Most methods store small integers plus a **scale factor** for each block of numbers. At run time, the kernel converts each block back to an approximate real value. | Llama 2 70B weights | Bytes per parameter | Approximate size | |---------------------|---------------------|------------------| | bf16 | 2 | 140 GB | | int8 | 1 | 70 GB | | 4-bit | about 0.5 (plus scales) | about 35–40 GB | ### Why quantization makes generation faster Decode is limited by memory bandwidth ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)). Half the bytes means about half the time to read the weights. So quantization raises speed as well as capacity, even if the arithmetic itself stays in 16-bit. ### What to quantize | Target | Effect | |--------|--------| | Weights only | The most common choice. It shrinks the model and speeds up decode. | | Weights and activations | Also speeds up compute-bound work such as prefill. It is harder to keep accurate. | | KV cache | Fits longer contexts and larger batches. | ### Two reference methods - **LLM.int8()** ([Dettmers et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339)) found that large models develop a few **outlier features** with very large values. A plain 8-bit format damages them. The method keeps the outlier dimensions in 16-bit and puts more than 99.9% of the values in 8-bit. The authors report no quality loss up to 175 B parameters. - **GPTQ** ([Frantar et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323)) is a one-time, post-training method. It uses a small calibration dataset to choose the rounding that does the least damage. It quantized 175 B-parameter models to 3–4 bits in about four GPU hours, with small accuracy loss. ### Trade-offs - Accuracy falls as bits fall. 8-bit is usually close to the original. 4-bit is a common practical balance. Below 4 bits, quality loss is often visible. - Post-training quantization (PTQ) needs no retraining. Quantization-aware training (QAT) trains the model with the low-bit format in the loop and usually keeps more quality. ## Sources - Hugging Face, *safetensors* repository — https://github.com/huggingface/safetensors - Hugging Face, *safetensors: metadata parsing* — https://huggingface.co/docs/safetensors/metadata_parsing - ggml project, *GGUF specification* — https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md - JFrog Security Research, *Data Scientists Targeted by Malicious Hugging Face ML Models with Silent Backdoor*, 2024 — https://jfrog.com/blog/data-scientists-targeted-by-malicious-hugging-face-ml-models-with-silent-backdoor/ - Dettmers et al., *LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339 - Frantar et al., *GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers*, ICLR 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323 ======= # 12 — Training Lifecycle **Scope:** the pipeline that produces the weights file, seen as a sequence of system stages. This document skips the math of the gradient. **Previous:** [11 Model files and quantization](11-model-files-and-quantization.md). **Next:** [13 Interpretability](13-interpretability.md). ## The weights file is a build artifact The weights ([02](02-tensors-and-weights.md)) are the output of a multi-stage pipeline. Each stage keeps the architecture and changes only the numbers. The `config.json` file stays the same from the first stage to the last. ```mermaid flowchart LR D1["Raw text corpus
(trillions of tokens)"] --> TK["1. Train tokenizer
(01)"] TK --> PT["2. Pretrain
next-token prediction"] D1 --> PT PT --> BASE[("Base model")] BASE --> SFT["3. Supervised fine-tuning
on demonstrations"] D2["Human-written
prompt/response pairs"] --> SFT SFT --> PREF["4. Preference tuning
RLHF or DPO"] D3["Human rankings
of model outputs"] --> PREF PREF --> CHAT[("Chat model")] CHAT --> POST["5. Optional post-processing
quantization (11), adapters"] ``` ## Stage 1: train the tokenizer The tokenizer trains first, on a sample of the corpus, and then stays frozen ([01](01-tokenizer.md)). Its vocabulary size fixes the shape of the embedding table and the output head. ## Stage 2: pretraining The model learns to predict the next token on a very large text corpus. **The training step** repeats millions of times: 1. **Forward pass.** Run a batch of text through the model. This is the same computation as inference ([00](00-big-picture.md)), but every position predicts its own next token at once. 2. **Loss.** Measure how much probability the model gave to the real next tokens. 3. **Backward pass.** Compute, for every weight, the direction that reduces the loss (the gradient). 4. **Optimizer update.** Move every weight a small step in that direction. **System profile:** - Training holds much more state than inference. With the Adam optimizer and mixed precision, each parameter needs about 16 bytes for weights, gradients, and optimizer state ([Rajbhandari et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)). The activations of the forward pass must also stay in memory for the backward pass. - So training needs data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism across thousands of GPUs ([09](09-scaling-across-devices.md)). **How much data?** [Hoffmann et al. (2022), "Chinchilla"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) found that, for a fixed compute budget, the model size and the data size should grow together. The popular summary is about 20 training tokens per parameter. That rule optimizes **training** cost only. A smaller model is cheaper to **serve**. So labs now train small models on far more data. Llama 3 8B trained on about 15 trillion tokens, far beyond the Chinchilla ratio ([Llama 3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)). The output of this stage is a **base model**. It continues text well, but it does not follow instructions reliably. ## Stage 3: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) The base model trains further on a smaller set of example conversations. People write ideal responses to prompts. This stage teaches the response style and the **chat template** format ([01](01-tokenizer.md)). The training step is the same as in pretraining. Only the data changes. ## Stage 4: preference tuning People compare pairs of model outputs and choose the better one. The model then trains to prefer the outputs that people prefer. **RLHF**, as described in InstructGPT ([Ouyang et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)), has three steps: 1. Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations (stage 3). 2. Train a separate **reward model** on human rankings. It learns to predict which output a person would prefer. 3. Fine-tune the language model with reinforcement learning (PPO) to raise the reward model's score. In human evaluations, outputs of the 1.3 B-parameter InstructGPT model were preferred to outputs of the 175 B-parameter GPT-3. For human preference, the post-training stages mattered more than a 100× difference in size. **DPO** ([Rafailov et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)) removes the separate reward model and the reinforcement learning loop. It trains directly on the preference pairs. This makes the pipeline simpler. ## Stage 5: optional post-processing - **Quantization** shrinks the model for serving ([11](11-model-files-and-quantization.md)). - **LoRA adapters** ([Hu et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)) fine-tune a model by training small add-on matrices and freezing the original weights. An adapter file is often only megabytes in size. A server can load one base model and switch between many adapters. ## Sources - Hoffmann et al., *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla)*, 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556 - Kaplan et al., *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361 - Ouyang et al., *Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155 - Rafailov et al., *Direct Preference Optimization*, NeurIPS 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290 - Hu et al., *LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models*, ICLR 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685 - Rajbhandari et al., *ZeRO*, SC 2020 — https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054 - Llama Team, *The Llama 3 Herd of Models*, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783 ======= # 13 — Interpretability: Features and Circuits **Scope:** what researchers find when they look inside an LLM: features, superposition, and circuits. This is the "debugger" view of the model. **Previous:** [12 Training lifecycle](12-training-lifecycle.md). **Next:** [14 Reasoning models](14-reasoning-models.md). ## Why a system designer should care The weights file has no comments and no symbol table. Interpretability research tries to recover the "source code" of the behavior from the weights. It matters for the same reasons a debugger matters: to explain a failure, to verify a safety property, and to change a behavior on purpose. ## Levels of description ```mermaid flowchart BT W["Weights
billions of numbers (02)"] --> N["Neurons
MLP hidden units (06)"] N --> F["Features
directions in activation space"] F --> C["Circuits
features connected by weights"] C --> B["Behavior
'the model answers Austin'"] ``` The neuron is the unit that the architecture defines. The **feature** is the unit that carries meaning. The research below explains why the two differ. ## Features are directions, not neurons [Olah et al. (2020), *Zoom In*](https://distill.pub/2020/circuits/zoom-in/) propose three claims from work on vision models: 1. **Features** are the basic units of a network. A feature corresponds to a **direction** in the space of activations. 2. Features connect through weights to form **circuits**. 3. Similar features and circuits appear in different models ("universality"). A direction can align with one neuron, but it does not have to. In LLMs, it usually does not. ## Superposition: more features than dimensions [Elhage et al. This is **superposition**. - The consequence is the **polysemantic neuron**: one neuron responds to several unrelated features. A system analogy: the residual stream ([04](04-transformer-block.md)) is a fixed-width bus, and the model compresses a much larger set of signals onto it. When researchers forced a "Golden Gate Bridge" feature to stay active, the model brought the bridge into unrelated answers ([*Golden Gate Claude*](https://www.anthropic.com/news/golden-gate-claude)). A caution from critics: a feature's label comes from its strongest examples.
