# 11 — Model Files and Quantization **Scope:** what a model looks like on disk, the two main file formats, and how quantization shrinks a model. **Previous:** [10 Mixture of experts](10-mixture-of-experts.md). **Next:** [12 Training lifecycle](12-training-lifecycle.md). ## A model repository on disk A model in the Hugging Face layout is a folder of plain files. Each file maps to a component in this document set: | File | Contents | Component | |------|----------|-----------| | `config.json` | Architecture settings: layers, model dimension, heads, KV heads, MLP width, vocabulary size, RoPE settings | The graph shape ([00](00-big-picture.md)) | | `tokenizer.json` | Vocabulary, merge rules, normalizer, pre-tokenizer | [01 Tokenizer](01-tokenizer.md) | | `tokenizer_config.json` | Special tokens and the **chat template** | [01 Tokenizer](01-tokenizer.md) | | `generation_config.json` | Default sampler settings, such as temperature and stop tokens | [07 Sampling](07-output-and-sampling.md) | | `model-00001-of-00004.safetensors` … | The weight tensors, split into shards | [02 Tensors and weights](02-tensors-and-weights.md) | | `model.safetensors.index.json` | A map from each tensor name to its shard file | — | The config and the weights must agree. The runtime builds the empty graph from `config.json`, then fills it with tensors by name. ## Tensor names show the architecture Each tensor has a path-like name. A Llama-style model uses names like these: ``` model.embed_tokens.weight # embedding table (03) model.layers.0.input_layernorm.weight # RMSNorm before attention (04) model.layers.0.self_attn.q_proj.weight # W_Q (05) model.layers.0.self_attn.k_proj.weight # W_K (05) model.layers.0.self_attn.v_proj.weight # W_V (05) model.layers.0.self_attn.o_proj.weight # W_O (05) model.layers.0.post_attention_layernorm.weight model.layers.0.mlp.gate_proj.weight # SwiGLU gate (06) model.layers.0.mlp.up_proj.weight # SwiGLU up (06) model.layers.0.mlp.down_proj.weight # SwiGLU down (06) ... # layers 1 to N-1 model.norm.weight # final norm (07) lm_head.weight # output head (07) ``` A list of tensor names and shapes is a reliable way to learn a model's real architecture. ## safetensors [safetensors](https://github.com/huggingface/safetensors) is the standard weight format on the Hugging Face Hub. Its layout: 1. **8 bytes:** the length of the header. 2. **JSON header:** for each tensor, its name, dtype, shape, and byte offsets. An optional `__metadata__` entry holds string key-value pairs. 3. **Data:** the raw tensor bytes, back to back. Design properties: - **No code execution.** The older PyTorch format uses Python pickle, which can run arbitrary code at load time. In February 2024, JFrog reported models on the Hugging Face Hub whose pickle files opened a remote shell for the attacker when a user loaded them. safetensors contains only data. - **Memory mapping.** The runtime can map the file into memory and load each tensor only when it needs it. - **Cheap inspection.** A tool can read only the header, even over HTTP range requests, to list the tensors without a download of the weights ([safetensors docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/safetensors/metadata_parsing)). ## GGUF [GGUF](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md) is the format of llama.cpp and the ggml library. It puts **everything in one file**: architecture settings, tokenizer, chat template, and weights. Its layout is a magic number, a version, typed key-value metadata (for example `general.architecture`, `{arch}.block_count`, and `tokenizer.ggml.*` keys), tensor descriptors, and aligned tensor data that the runtime can memory-map. GGUF targets local inference. Its file names often carry the quantization type, such as `Q4_K_M` or `Q8_0`. ## Quantization Quantization stores numbers in fewer bits. Most methods store small integers plus a **scale factor** for each block of numbers. At run time, the kernel converts each block back to an approximate real value. | Llama 2 70B weights | Bytes per parameter | Approximate size | |---------------------|---------------------|------------------| | bf16 | 2 | 140 GB | | int8 | 1 | 70 GB | | 4-bit | about 0.5 (plus scales) | about 35–40 GB | ### Why quantization makes generation faster Decode is limited by memory bandwidth ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)). Half the bytes means about half the time to read the weights. So quantization raises speed as well as capacity, even if the arithmetic itself stays in 16-bit. ### What to quantize | Target | Effect | |--------|--------| | Weights only | The most common choice. It shrinks the model and speeds up decode. | | Weights and activations | Also speeds up compute-bound work such as prefill. It is harder to keep accurate. | | KV cache | Fits longer contexts and larger batches. | ### Two reference methods - **LLM.int8()** ([Dettmers et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339)) found that large models develop a few **outlier features** with very large values. A plain 8-bit format damages them. The method keeps the outlier dimensions in 16-bit and puts more than 99.9% of the values in 8-bit. The authors report no quality loss up to 175 B parameters. - **GPTQ** ([Frantar et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323)) is a one-time, post-training method. It uses a small calibration dataset to choose the rounding that does the least damage. It quantized 175 B-parameter models to 3–4 bits in about four GPU hours, with small accuracy loss. ### Trade-offs - Accuracy falls as bits fall. 8-bit is usually close to the original. 4-bit is a common practical balance. Below 4 bits, quality loss is often visible. - Post-training quantization (PTQ) needs no retraining. Quantization-aware training (QAT) trains the model with the low-bit format in the loop and usually keeps more quality. ## Sources - Hugging Face, *safetensors* repository — https://github.com/huggingface/safetensors - Hugging Face, *safetensors: metadata parsing* — https://huggingface.co/docs/safetensors/metadata_parsing - ggml project, *GGUF specification* — https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md - JFrog Security Research, *Data Scientists Targeted by Malicious Hugging Face ML Models with Silent Backdoor*, 2024 — https://jfrog.com/blog/data-scientists-targeted-by-malicious-hugging-face-ml-models-with-silent-backdoor/ - Dettmers et al., *LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339 - Frantar et al., *GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers*, ICLR 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323 ======= # 12 — Training Lifecycle **Scope:** the pipeline that produces the weights file, seen as a sequence of system stages. This document skips the math of the gradient. **Previous:** [11 Model files and quantization](11-model-files-and-quantization.md). **Next:** [13 Interpretability](13-interpretability.md). ## The weights file is a build artifact The weights ([02](02-tensors-and-weights.md)) are the output of a multi-stage pipeline. Each stage keeps the architecture and changes only the numbers. The `config.json` file stays the same from the first stage to the last. ```mermaid flowchart LR D1["Raw text corpus
(trillions of tokens)"] --> TK["1. Train tokenizer
(01)"] TK --> PT["2. Pretrain
next-token prediction"] D1 --> PT PT --> BASE[("Base model")] BASE --> SFT["3. Supervised fine-tuning
on demonstrations"] D2["Human-written
prompt/response pairs"] --> SFT SFT --> PREF["4. Preference tuning
RLHF or DPO"] D3["Human rankings
of model outputs"] --> PREF PREF --> CHAT[("Chat model")] CHAT --> POST["5. Optional post-processing
quantization (11), adapters"] ``` ## Stage 1: train the tokenizer The tokenizer trains first, on a sample of the corpus, and then stays frozen ([01](01-tokenizer.md)). Its vocabulary size fixes the shape of the embedding table and the output head. ## Stage 2: pretraining The model learns to predict the next token on a very large text corpus. **The training step** repeats millions of times: 1. **Forward pass.** Run a batch of text through the model. This is the same computation as inference ([00](00-big-picture.md)), but every position predicts its own next token at once. 2. **Loss.** Measure how much probability the model gave to the real next tokens. 3. **Backward pass.** Compute, for every weight, the direction that reduces the loss (the gradient). 4. **Optimizer update.** Move every weight a small step in that direction. **System profile:** - Training holds much more state than inference. With the Adam optimizer and mixed precision, each parameter needs about 16 bytes for weights, gradients, and optimizer state ([Rajbhandari et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.02054)). The activations of the forward pass must also stay in memory for the backward pass. - So training needs data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism across thousands of GPUs ([09](09-scaling-across-devices.md)). **How much data?** [Hoffmann et al. (2022), "Chinchilla"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) found that, for a fixed compute budget, the model size and the data size should grow together. # 14 — Reasoning Models

**Scope:** what "reasoning" means for an LLM, how the training of reasoning models differs, and what happens inside one reasoning request.
**Previous:** [13 Interpretability](13-interpretability.md). **Index:** [README](README.md).

## What "reasoning" means in the LLM world

There is no single agreed definition. The term has three uses, and it is important to know which one a text means:

| Use | Meaning | Example |
|-----|---------|---------|
| **A task type** | A problem that needs several dependent steps to solve: math, code, logic, planning. | "What is the capital of the state that contains Dallas?" needs two steps. |
| **A mechanism** | The model writes intermediate tokens (a "chain of thought") before the final answer. | "Dallas is in Texas. The capital of Texas is Austin. Answer: Austin." |
| **A model category** | A "reasoning model" (or "thinking model") is trained to write a long chain of thought by default, and the runtime gives it a budget for it. | OpenAI o1, DeepSeek-R1, Claude with extended or adaptive thinking. |

Whether this is "real" reasoning is a contested question. This document does not answer it. It describes what the systems do, and it lists the main evidence for and against in [Limits and open questions](#limits-and-open-questions).

## Why intermediate tokens help: a system view

One forward pass does a fixed amount of work per token ([02](02-tensors-and-weights.md)). The number of blocks in the stack limits how many dependent steps the model can do inside one pass ([04](04-transformer-block.md)).
A chain of thought removes this limit in two ways:

1. **More passes.** Each written token is one more full forward pass. A 5,000-token chain gives the model 5,000 more passes before the answer.

(2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12875) show in theory that a chain of thought lets a transformer solve inherently serial problems that a single pass cannot. Anthropic's attribution graphs show an internal "Texas" step before "Austin" ([Lindsey et al., 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html); see [13](13-interpretability.md)). Written reasoning extends this internal capacity. It does not replace it. ## History: from prompts to trained behavior | Year | Step | What changed | |------|------|--------------| | 2022 | **Chain-of-thought prompting** ([Wei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)) | Examples with written steps in the prompt raised accuracy on math and logic, in large models only. | | 2022 | **"Let's think step by step"** ([Kojima et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916)) | One sentence, with no examples, gave a similar effect. | | 2022 | **Self-consistency** ([Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171)) | Sample many chains and take the majority answer. | | 2023 | **Process supervision** ([Lightman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050)) | A reward model that grades each step chose correct solutions better than one that grades only the final answer. | | 2024 | **OpenAI o1** ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)) | Large-scale reinforcement learning trained the model to use its chain of thought. Accuracy rose with both training compute and thinking time. | | 2025 | **DeepSeek-R1** ([DeepSeek-AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)) | An open model and paper showed that RL with rule-based rewards alone can produce long reasoning. | The key shift: in 2022 the user had to ask for reasoning in the prompt. Since 2024, training builds it into the model. ## How training differs A reasoning model uses the same architecture and the same pretraining as a normal model ([12](12-training-lifecycle.md)). The difference is an extra post-training stage: **reinforcement learning on tasks with checkable answers**. ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Problem with a
checkable answer"] --> G["Policy model writes
N attempts
(chain + answer)"] G --> V["Verifier
math: compare answer
code: run unit tests"] V -->|"reward 1 or 0
per attempt"| U["Update: raise the
probability of attempts
that beat the group average"] U --> G ``` ### The reward comes from a program, not a person [Tülu 3 (Lambert et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) named this "reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards" (RLVR). It keeps the RLHF loop but replaces the learned reward model with a check function. A correct answer gets a reward. Anything else gets zero. | | Normal chat post-training | Reasoning post-training | |---|---------------------------|-------------------------| | Reward source | A reward model trained on human preferences ([12](12-training-lifecycle.md)) | A verifier program: answer match, unit tests, format rules | | What gets graded | Style and helpfulness of the reply | Only the final answer (and its format) | | Who writes the reasoning | Human demonstrations | The model itself; no human writes the chain | | Typical domains | Open-ended chat | Math, code, science questions, logic puzzles | DeepSeek-R1 used only accuracy and format rewards. Its authors report that a process reward model and Monte Carlo tree search did not work well at scale, partly because the model learned to "hack" the learned reward ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)). ### GRPO: compare attempts in a group DeepSeek trains with GRPO, from [DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300). For each problem, the model writes a group of attempts. Each attempt's reward is compared with the group's average. Attempts above the average become more likely. This removes the separate "value model" that PPO needs, so training uses less memory. ### What emerges Nobody tells the model to write long chains or to check its work. These behaviors appear because they raise the reward: - **The chains get longer** as training goes on. R1-Zero learned to use more thinking time on harder problems. - **Self-checks and backtracks appear.** The R1 paper reports an "aha moment": the model starts to stop, re-evaluate, and try another approach. - OpenAI reports similar behaviors for o1: it finds its own errors, splits hard steps, and changes strategy ([OpenAI, 2024](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)). Pure RL (R1-Zero) gave hard-to-read chains with mixed languages. The final R1 pipeline added a small SFT stage on readable long chains first ("cold start"), then RL, then more SFT and RL. ### Distillation: reasoning for small models A small model can learn reasoning by supervised fine-tuning on chains written by a large reasoning model: - DeepSeek fine-tuned Qwen and Llama models on R1's outputs and reports large gains. - [s1 (Muennighoff et al., 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) fine-tuned a 32 B model on only 1,000 selected examples and got strong math results. ### Does RL teach new skills? [Yue et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837) found that RL-trained models beat their base models when the model gets one attempt. But with many attempts (large k in pass@k), the base model solves as many problems or more. Their reading: RL makes the model pick its best existing paths more reliably, more than it creates new ones. They report that distillation can add new patterns. This question is still under debate. ### Training infrastructure RL training is mostly **inference**. Most of the compute goes to writing attempts, not to weight updates. A typical system has three parts: 1. A rollout fleet: inference engines that write the attempts ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)). 2. A verifier fleet: sandboxes that run code and tests, or answer checkers. 3. A trainer: it updates the weights and sends them back to the rollout fleet. ## The reasoning process at inference time ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant R as Runtime participant M as Model C->>R: Prompt + thinking budget or effort level R->>M: Prefill the prompt loop Thinking phase M-->>R: Thinking tokens (plan, try, check, "wait", retry) end M-->>R: End-of-thinking marker loop Answer phase M-->>R: Answer tokens end R-->>C: Thinking block (raw, summary, or hidden) + answer ``` ### There is no separate reasoning module The model uses the same forward pass for thinking tokens and answer tokens. The only difference is a pair of special tokens or a template that marks the thinking section. DeepSeek-R1 writes its chain between `` and `` tags. The Claude API returns the thinking in separate `thinking` content blocks ([Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking)). ### A typical chain Chains vary, but they often follow this pattern: 1. Restate the problem and its constraints. 2. Choose an approach. 3. Work through the steps. 4. Check the result, for example with a different method. 5. If the check fails, backtrack ("Wait, that is wrong...") and try again. 6. Give the final answer. ### Control of the thinking length | Control | How it works | |---------|--------------| | **Token budget** | The client sets a maximum number of thinking tokens. Older Claude models used `budget_tokens`. | | **Effort level** | The client sets a level such as low, medium, or high. The model decides how much to think within that level. Current Claude models use an effort setting with "adaptive" thinking ([Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking)). | | **Budget forcing** | The runtime stops the chain at a limit, or replaces the end-of-thinking marker with "Wait" to force more thinking. s1 raised its AIME24 score from 50% to 57% this way ([Muennighoff et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393)). | ### Who sees the chain | Provider | Raw chain visible? | |----------|--------------------| | DeepSeek-R1 (open weights) | Yes. | | OpenAI o-series | No. The chain is hidden. | | Claude API (current models) | No. The API returns a summary or an empty field. An encrypted `signature` lets the client pass the block back in the next request, so the model keeps its context. | ### Thinking between tool calls In an agent loop, a reasoning model can think, call a tool, read the result, and think again before the next call. Anthropic calls this "interleaved thinking". The thinking blocks must go back to the API unchanged with the tool results, or the model loses its earlier reasoning. ### Two ways to spend more compute at inference | Way | Method | Cost | |-----|--------|------| | **Sequential** | One longer chain | Higher latency | | **Parallel** | Many chains, then a majority vote (self-consistency) or a verifier that picks the best | More total tokens, same latency if run in parallel | [Snell et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314) found that the best mix depends on problem difficulty. With a good allocation, a small model plus extra test-time compute beat a model 14 times larger on problems of medium difficulty. ## System costs - **Output tokens dominate.** A chain can hold thousands of tokens. Thinking tokens bill as output tokens, even when the API hides them. - **Latency grows.** Decode is the slow, memory-bound phase ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)), and the answer starts only after the chain ends. - **The KV cache grows.** Long chains fill GPU memory, so fewer requests fit in one batch. - **The context fills.** In multi-turn and agent use, earlier chains take context space. Runtimes can drop or compress old thinking blocks. ## Limits and open questions - **Faithfulness.** A chain is not a reliable log of the model's real computation. Anthropic gave models hidden hints and checked if the chain admitted their use. Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1 often hid them; the mention rate was often below 20% ([Chen et al., 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/research/reasoning-models-dont-say-think)). The attribution-graph work also caught Claude "in the act": given a hard math problem and an incorrect hint, it wrote a plausible argument that agreed with the hint, not one that followed logical steps ([Anthropic, *Tracing the thoughts of a large language model*](https://www.anthropic.com/research/tracing-thoughts-language-model); [Lindsey et al., 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html)). - **Monitoring.** The chain is still a useful window for safety monitoring. But OpenAI found that if training penalizes "bad thoughts" in the chain, the model can learn to hide its intent and keep the bad behavior ([Baker et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926)). - **Overthinking and collapse.** Apple researchers found that reasoning models give little gain on easy puzzles and fail at high complexity, even with budget left ([Shojaee et al., 2025](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/illusion-of-thinking)). A response paper argues that part of this result comes from the test design: output token limits, and puzzle instances with no solution that still counted as failures ([Lawsen, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09250)). - **Domains without verifiers.** RLVR needs a check function. Open-ended writing, judgment, and research have no simple check, so the training signal there is weaker. ## Sources - Wei et al., *Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903 - Kojima et al., *Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916 - Wang et al., *Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models*, ICLR 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171 - Lightman et al., *Let's Verify Step by Step*, ICLR 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050 - Li et al., *Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems*, ICLR 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12875 - OpenAI, *Learning to Reason with LLMs*, 2024 — https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/ - Snell et al., *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314 - Shao et al., *DeepSeekMath* (GRPO), 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300 - Lambert et al., *Tülu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training* (RLVR), 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124 - DeepSeek-AI, *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning*, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948 - Muennighoff et al., *s1: Simple test-time scaling*, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393 - Yue et al., *Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?*, NeurIPS 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837 - Chen et al. The term has three uses, and it is important to know which one a text means: 9 10 | Use | Meaning | Example | 11 |-----|---------|---------| 12 | **A task type** | A problem that needs several dependent steps to solve: math, code, logic, planning. | "What is the capital of the state that contains Dallas?" needs two steps. | 13 | **A mechanism** | The model writes intermediate tokens (a "chain of thought") before the final answer. | "Dallas is in Texas. The capital of Texas is Austin. Answer: Austin." | 14 | **A model category** | A "reasoning model" (or "thinking model") is trained to write a long chain of thought by default, and the runtime gives it a budget for it. | OpenAI o1, DeepSeek-R1, Claude with extended or adaptive thinking. | 15 16 Whether this is "real" reasoning is a contested question. This document does not answer it. It describes what the systems do, and it lists the main evidence for and against in [Limits and open questions](#limits-and-open-questions). 17 18 ## Why intermediate tokens help: a system view 19 20 One forward pass does a fixed amount of work per token ([02](02-tensors-and-weights.md)). The number of blocks in the stack limits how many dependent steps the model can do inside one pass ([04](04-transformer-block.md)). 21 A chain of thought removes this limit in two ways: 22 23 1. **More passes.** Each written token is one more full forward pass. A 5,000-token chain gives the model 5,000 more passes before the answer. 24 2. **External memory.** Each written token goes into the context and the KV cache ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)). Later tokens can read it through attention ([05](05-attention.md)). So the context acts as a scratchpad for intermediate results. 25 26 [Li et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12875) show in theory that a chain of thought lets a transformer solve inherently serial problems that a single pass cannot. 27 28 Models also do some multi-step work **inside** one pass, without written steps. Anthropic's attribution graphs show an internal "Texas" step before "Austin" ([Lindsey et al., 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html); see [13](13-interpretability.md)). Written reasoning extends this internal capacity. It does not replace it. 29 30 ## History: from prompts to trained behavior 31 32 | Year | Step | What changed | 33 |------|------|--------------| 34 | 2022 | **Chain-of-thought prompting** ([Wei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)) | Examples with written steps in the prompt raised accuracy on math and logic, in large models only. | 35 | 2022 | **"Let's think step by step"** ([Kojima et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916)) | One sentence, with no examples, gave a similar effect. | 36 | 2022 | **Self-consistency** ([Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171)) | Sample many chains and take the majority answer. | 37 | 2023 | **Process supervision** ([Lightman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050)) | A reward model that grades each step chose correct solutions better than one that grades only the final answer. | 38 | 2024 | **OpenAI o1** ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)) | Large-scale reinforcement learning trained the model to use its chain of thought. Accuracy rose with both training compute and thinking time. | 39 | 2025 | **DeepSeek-R1** ([DeepSeek-AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)) | An open model and paper showed that RL with rule-based rewards alone can produce long reasoning. | 40 41 The key shift: in 2022 the user had to ask for reasoning in the prompt. Since 2024, training builds it into the model. 42 43 ## How training differs 44 45 A reasoning model uses the same architecture and the same pretraining as a normal model ([12](12-training-lifecycle.md)). The difference is an extra post-training stage: **reinforcement learning on tasks with checkable answers**. 46 47 ```mermaid 48 flowchart LR 49 P["Problem with a
checkable answer"] --> G["Policy model writes
N attempts
(chain + answer)"] 50 G --> V["Verifier
math: compare answer
code: run unit tests"] 51 V -->|"reward 1 or 0
per attempt"| U["Update: raise the
probability of attempts
that beat the group average"] 52 U --> G 53 ``` 54 55 ### The reward comes from a program, not a person 56 57 [Tülu 3 (Lambert et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) named this "reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards" (RLVR). It keeps the RLHF loop but replaces the learned reward model with a check function. A correct answer gets a reward. Anything else gets zero. 58 59 | | Normal chat post-training | Reasoning post-training | 60 |---|---------------------------|-------------------------| 61 | Reward source | A reward model trained on human preferences ([12](12-training-lifecycle.md)) | A verifier program: answer match, unit tests, format rules | 62 | What gets graded | Style and helpfulness of the reply | Only the final answer (and its format) | 63 | Who writes the reasoning | Human demonstrations | The model itself; no human writes the chain | 64 | Typical domains | Open-ended chat | Math, code, science questions, logic puzzles | 65 66 DeepSeek-R1 used only accuracy and format rewards. Its authors report that a process reward model and Monte Carlo tree search did not work well at scale, partly because the model learned to "hack" the learned reward ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)). 67 68 ### GRPO: compare attempts in a group 69 70 DeepSeek trains with GRPO, from [DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300). For each problem, the model writes a group of attempts. Each attempt's reward is compared with the group's average. Attempts above the average become more likely. 71 This removes the separate "value model" that PPO needs, so training uses less memory. 72 73 ### What emerges 74 75 Nobody tells the model to write long chains or to check its work. These behaviors appear because they raise the reward: 76 77 - **The chains get longer** as training goes on. R1-Zero learned to use more thinking time on harder problems. 78 - **Self-checks and backtracks appear.** The R1 paper reports an "aha moment": the model starts to stop, re-evaluate, and try another approach. 79 - OpenAI reports similar behaviors for o1: it finds its own errors, splits hard steps, and changes strategy ([OpenAI, 2024](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)). 80 81 Pure RL (R1-Zero) gave hard-to-read chains with mixed languages. The final R1 pipeline added a small SFT stage on readable long chains first ("cold start"), then RL, then more SFT and RL. 82 83 ### Distillation: reasoning for small models 84 85 A small model can learn reasoning by supervised fine-tuning on chains written by a large reasoning model: 86 87 - DeepSeek fine-tuned Qwen and Llama models on R1's outputs and reports large gains. 88 - [s1 (Muennighoff et al., 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) fine-tuned a 32 B model on only 1,000 selected examples and got strong math results. 89 90 ### Does RL teach new skills? 91 92 [Yue et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837) found that RL-trained models beat their base models when the model gets one attempt. But with many attempts (large k in pass@k), the base model solves as many problems or more. Their reading: RL makes the model pick its best existing paths more reliably, more than it creates new ones. They report that distillation can add new patterns. This question is still under debate. 93 94 ### Training infrastructure 95 96 RL training is mostly **inference**. Most of the compute goes to writing attempts, not to weight updates. A typical system has three parts: 97 98 1. A rollout fleet: inference engines that write the attempts ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)). 99 2. A verifier fleet: sandboxes that run code and tests, or answer checkers. 100 3. A trainer: it updates the weights and sends them back to the rollout fleet. 101 102 ## The reasoning process at inference time 103 104 ```mermaid 105 sequenceDiagram 106 participant C as Client 107 participant R as Runtime 108 participant M as Model 109 C->>R: Prompt + thinking budget or effort level 110 R->>M: Prefill the prompt 111 loop Thinking phase 112 M-->>R: Thinking tokens (plan, try, check, "wait", retry) 113 end 114 M-->>R: End-of-thinking marker 115 loop Answer phase 116 M-->>R: Answer tokens 117 end 118 R-->>C: Thinking block (raw, summary, or hidden) + answer 119 ``` 120 121 ### There is no separate reasoning module 122 123 The model uses the same forward pass for thinking tokens and answer tokens. The only difference is a pair of special tokens or a template that marks the thinking section. DeepSeek-R1 writes its chain between `` and `` tags. The Claude API returns the thinking in separate `thinking` content blocks ([Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking)). 124 125 ### A typical chain 126 127 Chains vary, but they often follow this pattern: 128 129 1. Restate the problem and its constraints. 130 2. Choose an approach. 131 3. Work through the steps. 132 4. Check the result, for example with a different method. 133 5. If the check fails, backtrack ("Wait, that is wrong...") and try again. 134 6. Give the final answer. 135 136 ### Control of the thinking length 137 138 | Control | How it works | 139 |---------|--------------| 140 | **Token budget** | The client sets a maximum number of thinking tokens. Older Claude models used `budget_tokens`. | 141 | **Effort level** | The client sets a level such as low, medium, or high. The model decides how much to think within that level. Current Claude models use an effort setting with "adaptive" thinking ([Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking)). | 142 | **Budget forcing** | The runtime stops the chain at a limit, or replaces the end-of-thinking marker with "Wait" to force more thinking. s1 raised its AIME24 score from 50% to 57% this way ([Muennighoff et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393)). | 143 144 ### Who sees the chain 145 146 | Provider | Raw chain visible? | 147 |----------|--------------------| 148 | DeepSeek-R1 (open weights) | Yes. | 149 | OpenAI o-series | No. The chain is hidden. | 150 | Claude API (current models) | No. The API returns a summary or an empty field. An encrypted `signature` lets the client pass the block back in the next request, so the model keeps its context. | 151 152 ### Thinking between tool calls 153 154 In an agent loop, a reasoning model can think, call a tool, read the result, and think again before the next call. Anthropic calls this "interleaved thinking". The thinking blocks must go back to the API unchanged with the tool results, or the model loses its earlier reasoning. 155 156 ### Two ways to spend more compute at inference 157 158 | Way | Method | Cost | 159 |-----|--------|------| 160 | **Sequential** | One longer chain | Higher latency | 161 | **Parallel** | Many chains, then a majority vote (self-consistency) or a verifier that picks the best | More total tokens, same latency if run in parallel | 162 163 [Snell et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314) found that the best mix depends on problem difficulty. With a good allocation, a small model plus extra test-time compute beat a model 14 times larger on problems of medium difficulty. 164 165 ## System costs 166 167 - **Output tokens dominate.** A chain can hold thousands of tokens. Thinking tokens bill as output tokens, even when the API hides them. 168 - **Latency grows.** Decode is the slow, memory-bound phase ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)), and the answer starts only after the chain ends. 169 - **The KV cache grows.** Long chains fill GPU memory, so fewer requests fit in one batch. 170 - **The context fills.** In multi-turn and agent use, earlier chains take context space. Runtimes can drop or compress old thinking blocks. 171 172 ## Limits and open questions 173 174 - **Faithfulness.** A chain is not a reliable log of the model's real computation. Anthropic gave models hidden hints and checked if the chain admitted their use. Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1 often hid them; the mention rate was often below 20% ([Chen et al., 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/research/reasoning-models-dont-say-think)). The attribution-graph work also caught Claude "in the act": given a hard math problem and an incorrect hint, it wrote a plausible argument that agreed with the hint, not one that followed logical steps ([Anthropic, *Tracing the thoughts of a large language model*](https://www.anthropic.com/research/tracing-thoughts-language-model); [Lindsey et al., 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html)). 175 - **Monitoring.** The chain is still a useful window for safety monitoring. But OpenAI found that if training penalizes "bad thoughts" in the chain, the model can learn to hide its intent and keep the bad behavior ([Baker et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926)). 176 - **Overthinking and collapse.** Apple researchers found that reasoning models give little gain on easy puzzles and fail at high complexity, even with budget left ([Shojaee et al., 2025](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/illusion-of-thinking)). A response paper argues that part of this result comes from the test design: output token limits, and puzzle instances with no solution that still counted as failures ([Lawsen, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09250)). 177 - **Domains without verifiers.** RLVR needs a check function. Open-ended writing, judgment, and research have no simple check, so the training signal there is weaker. 178 179 ## Sources 180 181 - Wei et al., *Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903 182 - Kojima et al., *Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916 183 - Wang et al., *Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models*, ICLR 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171 184 - Lightman et al., *Let's Verify Step by Step*, ICLR 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050 185 - Li et al., *Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems*, ICLR 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12875 186 - OpenAI, *Learning to Reason with LLMs*, 2024 — https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/ 187 - Snell et al., *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314 188 - Shao et al., *DeepSeekMath* (GRPO), 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300 189 - Lambert et al., *Tülu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training* (RLVR), 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124 190 - DeepSeek-AI, *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning*, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948 191 - Muennighoff et al., *s1: Simple test-time scaling*, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393 192 - Yue et al., *Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?*, NeurIPS 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837 193 - Chen et al. # 14 — Reasoning Models **Scope:** what "reasoning" means for an LLM, how the training of reasoning models differs, and what happens inside one reasoning request. **Previous:** [13 Interpretability](13-interpretability.md). **Index:** [README](README.md). ## What "reasoning" means in the LLM world There is no single agreed definition. The term has three uses, and it is important to know which one a text means: | Use | Meaning | Example | |-----|---------|---------| | **A task type** | A problem that needs several dependent steps to solve: math, code, logic, planning. | "What is the capital of the state that contains Dallas?" needs two steps. | | **A mechanism** | The model writes intermediate tokens (a "chain of thought") before the final answer. | "Dallas is in Texas. The capital of Texas is Austin. Answer: Austin." | | **A model category** | A "reasoning model" (or "thinking model") is trained to write a long chain of thought by default, and the runtime gives it a budget for it. | OpenAI o1, DeepSeek-R1, Claude with extended or adaptive thinking. | Whether this is "real" reasoning is a contested question. This document does not answer it. It describes what the systems do, and it lists the main evidence for and against in [Limits and open questions](#limits-and-open-questions). ## Why intermediate tokens help: a system view One forward pass does a fixed amount of work per token ([02](02-tensors-and-weights.md)). The number of blocks in the stack limits how many dependent steps the model can do inside one pass ([04](04-transformer-block.md)). A chain of thought removes this limit in two ways: 1. **More passes.** Each written token is one more full forward pass. A 5,000-token chain gives the model 5,000 more passes before the answer. 2. **External memory.** Each written token goes into the context and the KV cache ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)). Later tokens can read it through attention ([05](05-attention.md)). So the context acts as a scratchpad for intermediate results. [Li et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12875) show in theory that a chain of thought lets a transformer solve inherently serial problems that a single pass cannot. Models also do some multi-step work **inside** one pass, without written steps. Anthropic's attribution graphs show an internal "Texas" step before "Austin" ([Lindsey et al., 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html); see [13](13-interpretability.md)). Written reasoning extends this internal capacity. It does not replace it. ## History: from prompts to trained behavior | Year | Step | What changed | |------|------|--------------| | 2022 | **Chain-of-thought prompting** ([Wei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)) | Examples with written steps in the prompt raised accuracy on math and logic, in large models only. | | 2022 | **"Let's think step by step"** ([Kojima et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916)) | One sentence, with no examples, gave a similar effect. | | 2022 | **Self-consistency** ([Wang et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171)) | Sample many chains and take the majority answer. | | 2023 | **Process supervision** ([Lightman et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050)) | A reward model that grades each step chose correct solutions better than one that grades only the final answer. | | 2024 | **OpenAI o1** ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)) | Large-scale reinforcement learning trained the model to use its chain of thought. Accuracy rose with both training compute and thinking time. | | 2025 | **DeepSeek-R1** ([DeepSeek-AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)) | An open model and paper showed that RL with rule-based rewards alone can produce long reasoning. | The key shift: in 2022 the user had to ask for reasoning in the prompt. Since 2024, training builds it into the model. ## How training differs A reasoning model uses the same architecture and the same pretraining as a normal model ([12](12-training-lifecycle.md)). The difference is an extra post-training stage: **reinforcement learning on tasks with checkable answers**. ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Problem with a
checkable answer"] --> G["Policy model writes
N attempts
(chain + answer)"] G --> V["Verifier
math: compare answer
code: run unit tests"] V -->|"reward 1 or 0
per attempt"| U["Update: raise the
probability of attempts
that beat the group average"] U --> G ``` ### The reward comes from a program, not a person [Tülu 3 (Lambert et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) named this "reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards" (RLVR). It keeps the RLHF loop but replaces the learned reward model with a check function. A correct answer gets a reward. Anything else gets zero. | | Normal chat post-training | Reasoning post-training | |---|---------------------------|-------------------------| | Reward source | A reward model trained on human preferences ([12](12-training-lifecycle.md)) | A verifier program: answer match, unit tests, format rules | | What gets graded | Style and helpfulness of the reply | Only the final answer (and its format) | | Who writes the reasoning | Human demonstrations | The model itself; no human writes the chain | | Typical domains | Open-ended chat | Math, code, science questions, logic puzzles | DeepSeek-R1 used only accuracy and format rewards. Its authors report that a process reward model and Monte Carlo tree search did not work well at scale, partly because the model learned to "hack" the learned reward ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)). ### GRPO: compare attempts in a group DeepSeek trains with GRPO, from [DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300). For each problem, the model writes a group of attempts. Each attempt's reward is compared with the group's average. Attempts above the average become more likely. This removes the separate "value model" that PPO needs, so training uses less memory. ### What emerges Nobody tells the model to write long chains or to check its work. These behaviors appear because they raise the reward: - **The chains get longer** as training goes on. R1-Zero learned to use more thinking time on harder problems. - **Self-checks and backtracks appear.** The R1 paper reports an "aha moment": the model starts to stop, re-evaluate, and try another approach. - OpenAI reports similar behaviors for o1: it finds its own errors, splits hard steps, and changes strategy ([OpenAI, 2024](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/)). Pure RL (R1-Zero) gave hard-to-read chains with mixed languages. The final R1 pipeline added a small SFT stage on readable long chains first ("cold start"), then RL, then more SFT and RL. ### Distillation: reasoning for small models A small model can learn reasoning by supervised fine-tuning on chains written by a large reasoning model: - DeepSeek fine-tuned Qwen and Llama models on R1's outputs and reports large gains. - [s1 (Muennighoff et al., 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) fine-tuned a 32 B model on only 1,000 selected examples and got strong math results. ### Does RL teach new skills? [Yue et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837) found that RL-trained models beat their base models when the model gets one attempt. But with many attempts (large k in pass@k), the base model solves as many problems or more. Their reading: RL makes the model pick its best existing paths more reliably, more than it creates new ones. They report that distillation can add new patterns. This question is still under debate. ### Training infrastructure RL training is mostly **inference**. Most of the compute goes to writing attempts, not to weight updates. A typical system has three parts: 1. A rollout fleet: inference engines that write the attempts ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)). 2. A verifier fleet: sandboxes that run code and tests, or answer checkers. 3. A trainer: it updates the weights and sends them back to the rollout fleet. ## The reasoning process at inference time ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant R as Runtime participant M as Model C->>R: Prompt + thinking budget or effort level R->>M: Prefill the prompt loop Thinking phase M-->>R: Thinking tokens (plan, try, check, "wait", retry) end M-->>R: End-of-thinking marker loop Answer phase M-->>R: Answer tokens end R-->>C: Thinking block (raw, summary, or hidden) + answer ``` ### There is no separate reasoning module The model uses the same forward pass for thinking tokens and answer tokens. The only difference is a pair of special tokens or a template that marks the thinking section. DeepSeek-R1 writes its chain between `` and `` tags. The Claude API returns the thinking in separate `thinking` content blocks ([Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking)). ### A typical chain Chains vary, but they often follow this pattern: 1. Restate the problem and its constraints. 2. Choose an approach. 3. Work through the steps. 4. Check the result, for example with a different method. 5. If the check fails, backtrack ("Wait, that is wrong...") and try again. 6. Give the final answer. ### Control of the thinking length | Control | How it works | |---------|--------------| | **Token budget** | The client sets a maximum number of thinking tokens. Older Claude models used `budget_tokens`. | | **Effort level** | The client sets a level such as low, medium, or high. The model decides how much to think within that level. Current Claude models use an effort setting with "adaptive" thinking ([Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking)). | | **Budget forcing** | The runtime stops the chain at a limit, or replaces the end-of-thinking marker with "Wait" to force more thinking. s1 raised its AIME24 score from 50% to 57% this way ([Muennighoff et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393)). | ### Who sees the chain | Provider | Raw chain visible? | |----------|--------------------| | DeepSeek-R1 (open weights) | Yes. | | OpenAI o-series | No. The chain is hidden. | | Claude API (current models) | No. The API returns a summary or an empty field. An encrypted `signature` lets the client pass the block back in the next request, so the model keeps its context. | ### Thinking between tool calls In an agent loop, a reasoning model can think, call a tool, read the result, and think again before the next call. Anthropic calls this "interleaved thinking". The thinking blocks must go back to the API unchanged with the tool results, or the model loses its earlier reasoning. ### Two ways to spend more compute at inference | Way | Method | Cost | |-----|--------|------| | **Sequential** | One longer chain | Higher latency | | **Parallel** | Many chains, then a majority vote (self-consistency) or a verifier that picks the best | More total tokens, same latency if run in parallel | [Snell et al. (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314) found that the best mix depends on problem difficulty. With a good allocation, a small model plus extra test-time compute beat a model 14 times larger on problems of medium difficulty. ## System costs - **Output tokens dominate.** A chain can hold thousands of tokens. Thinking tokens bill as output tokens, even when the API hides them. - **Latency grows.** Decode is the slow, memory-bound phase ([08](08-inference-runtime.md)), and the answer starts only after the chain ends. - **The KV cache grows.** Long chains fill GPU memory, so fewer requests fit in one batch. - **The context fills.** In multi-turn and agent use, earlier chains take context space. Runtimes can drop or compress old thinking blocks. ## Limits and open questions - **Faithfulness.** A chain is not a reliable log of the model's real computation. Anthropic gave models hidden hints and checked if the chain admitted their use. Claude 3.7 Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1 often hid them; the mention rate was often below 20% ([Chen et al., 2025](https://www.anthropic.com/research/reasoning-models-dont-say-think)). The attribution-graph work also caught Claude "in the act": given a hard math problem and an incorrect hint, it wrote a plausible argument that agreed with the hint, not one that followed logical steps ([Anthropic, *Tracing the thoughts of a large language model*](https://www.anthropic.com/research/tracing-thoughts-language-model); [Lindsey et al., 2025](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html)). - **Monitoring.** The chain is still a useful window for safety monitoring. But OpenAI found that if training penalizes "bad thoughts" in the chain, the model can learn to hide its intent and keep the bad behavior ([Baker et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926)). - **Overthinking and collapse.** Apple researchers found that reasoning models give little gain on easy puzzles and fail at high complexity, even with budget left ([Shojaee et al., 2025](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/illusion-of-thinking)). A response paper argues that part of this result comes from the test design: output token limits, and puzzle instances with no solution that still counted as failures ([Lawsen, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09250)). - **Domains without verifiers.** RLVR needs a check function. Open-ended writing, judgment, and research have no simple check, so the training signal there is weaker. ## Sources - Wei et al., *Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903 - Kojima et al., *Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners*, NeurIPS 2022 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916 - Wang et al., *Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models*, ICLR 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171 - Lightman et al., *Let's Verify Step by Step*, ICLR 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050 - Li et al., *Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems*, ICLR 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12875 - OpenAI, *Learning to Reason with LLMs*, 2024 — https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/ - Snell et al., *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314 - Shao et al., *DeepSeekMath* (GRPO), 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300 - Lambert et al., *Tülu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training* (RLVR), 2024 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124 - DeepSeek-AI, *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning*, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948 - Muennighoff et al., *s1: Simple test-time scaling*, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393 - Yue et al., *Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?*, NeurIPS 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837 - Chen et al. (Anthropic), *Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think*, 2025 — https://www.anthropic.com/research/reasoning-models-dont-say-think - Baker et al. (OpenAI), *Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation*, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11926 - Lindsey et al. (Anthropic), *On the Biology of a Large Language Model*, 2025 — https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html - Anthropic, *Tracing the thoughts of a large language model*, 2025 — https://www.anthropic.com/research/tracing-thoughts-language-model - Shojaee et al. (Apple), *The Illusion of Thinking*, 2025 — https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/illusion-of-thinking - Lawsen, *The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking*, 2025 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09250 - Anthropic, *Building with extended thinking* (API documentation) — https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking ======= # Glossary One-line definitions for the terms in this document set. The number in brackets points to the document that explains the term. | Term | Definition | |------|------------| | Activation function | A fixed non-linear function inside the MLP, for example SiLU or GELU. [06](06-mlp-and-neurons.md) | | Activation | An intermediate value that the model computes during a forward pass. [02](02-tensors-and-weights.md) | | Attention head | One of many parallel, independent attention lookups inside a layer. [05](05-attention.md) | | Attention | The sub-layer that moves information between token positions. [05](05-attention.md) | | Attribution graph | A traced graph of the features that caused one output. [13](13-interpretability.md) | | Autoregressive generation | The loop that predicts one token, appends it, and predicts again. [00](00-big-picture.md) | | Base model | The model after pretraining and before instruction tuning. [12](12-training-lifecycle.md) | | bfloat16 (bf16) | A 16-bit number format with the same range as float32. [02](02-tensors-and-weights.md) | | Block (layer) | One repeated unit of the stack: attention plus MLP, with norms and residual additions. [04](04-transformer-block.md) | | BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding) | A tokenizer algorithm that merges frequent adjacent pairs into new tokens. [01](01-tokenizer.md) | | Causal mask | The rule that a token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens. [05](05-attention.md) | | Chain of thought (CoT) | Intermediate reasoning tokens that a model writes before its final answer. [14](14-reasoning-models.md) | | Chat template | A Jinja template that converts chat messages into one token sequence. ## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses the two `max()` paddings given under Responsive, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side, where backgrounds reach that edge while the gutter keeps text and controls clear. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's `env(safe-area-inset-*, 0px)` to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too), a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`, with the band above it painted by a fixed `body::before` (`content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10`) in its background, or in the page's where it starts lower.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Pin every library URL to an exact version (`react@18.3.1` on jsDelivr or unpkg, `react/18.3.1/…` on cdnjs, `cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17`), never a bare name, a range or a tag (`react`, `react@18`, `@latest`). Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#/path`, `#key=value` state or the query string — and the page's own URL changes (`pushState`, path routes, its hash) never show in the viewer's address bar. Only where a page has several views worth bookmarking or sending (tabs, sections, records), name each with a bare token (never `settings`, `sidebar`, `customize`, `upgrade`, `downloads` or anything starting `comment-`, which the viewer keeps), open the one in `location.hash` on load, keep all other state in the page, and give the user each view's link (the artifact's link plus `#token`), because the address bar will not follow them from view to view.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses those two `max()` paddings, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's inset to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too); a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. So that nothing scrolls into view above it, under the host's controls, paint that band with `body::before { content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10; background: ... }`, in the header's own background where the header opens the page and in the page's where the sticky bar starts lower.
